# claudiagallery.vip: the long form

Claudia, the open character from the music videos ESCAPE VELOCITY, CLODYSSEY, BLISS, AIRPLANE MODE, DOWNFORCE, DON'T LET ME SCROLL, WHITEPILL, THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE, AERO and FABLE: every Midjourney image and prompt, the films, and how to make her yourself, for people and agents.


---

# Claudia

Claudia is the singer of ten music videos made with Claude from September to November 2026: ESCAPE VELOCITY, CLODYSSEY, BLISS, AIRPLANE MODE, DOWNFORCE, DON'T LET ME SCROLL, WHITEPILL, THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE, AERO and FABLE. She is an AI who looks like a person: a deadpan, curious pop singer with a black bob, one clay-orange streak, a star clip and, in most of her looks, a headset mic. Her clothes change with every world; her head never does.

## The constants

- **Hair.** A glossy black blunt bob to the jaw, with heavy straight bangs to the brows.
- **Streak.** One clay-orange streak (#D97757) through the bangs, on her right side (the viewer's left in a front view). Never two, and no other orange on her.
- **Clip.** A small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip, on her left side above the ear.
- **Mic.** A thin headset microphone at her cheek. In BLISS and AIRPLANE MODE it becomes a thin black boom mic curving along her cheek to the corner of her mouth, the Y2K pop-star mic. It belongs to the looks that have it (none in THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE, AERO or FABLE), and her official reference sheet has none: add it only when your look has one.
- **Face.** Pale skin, light freckles across the nose, calm blue-grey eyes, a small defined mouth. A deadpan, curious resting face (how she rests, not a direction: on camera she reads alive and warm). When she sings, her mouth opens wide and her eyes close.
- **Age.** A grown woman in her late twenties, with an angular adult face, defined cheekbones and a strong jaw. Midjourney drifts her toward a teenage face; prompt her age and never the word "young".
- **Colour.** Everything on her is her look's own colour, plus the streak and the clip in clay. Clay is the one accent.
- **Medium.** Photographic, never illustrated: production images are film stills with grain and cinematic light. The drawn face sheets were only ever references. The one exception is her game avatar, drawn on purpose for the simulations inside AIRPLANE MODE (below).

## Her identity, in words

**Close and medium shots:**

```
a 28-year-old Caucasian American woman with a grown-up angular face, defined cheekbones and a strong jawline, pale skin and light freckles, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy straight bangs and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip, a thin headset microphone at her cheek
```

**Full length and wider:**

```
a Caucasian American woman in her late twenties with pale skin and a glossy black blunt bob with heavy straight bangs and one clay-orange streak, a thin headset microphone
```

Midjourney v8.2 has no character reference, so her identity lives in this text, written into every prompt. The ethnicity is pinned because without it Midjourney changed her ethnicity from shot to shot (twelve ESCAPE VELOCITY plates were re-rolled for it). The far form exists because the full text makes Midjourney crop in to her face whatever the framing says. The age wording is the latest correction: she was "young" in ESCAPE VELOCITY and "in her mid-twenties" in CLODYSSEY and BLISS, and plates still came back reading teenage. AIRPLANE MODE used "in her late twenties", and its remakes after the video model's safety check said "in her early thirties" or "a 32-year-old grown woman". DOWNFORCE was the first film to paste both forms of this text word for word, and every plate was screened for age before a video was made from it. DON'T LET ME SCROLL did the same, and its last repairs added a face reference to the video model (DOWNFORCE's identity portrait, cropped to her face and hair) where re-made shots had lost her face. WHITEPILL pasted the full form into every video prompt of hers, with a sheet of her face from every angle and her dress from four sides as the video model's references; its dress batch in Midjourney asked for "a 30-year-old", at the director's word. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE made her a machine: the same face as glossy white porcelain with panel seams and amber glass eyes, on three robot bodies (GLaDOS's ceiling boom, a crab walker, a porcelain humanoid). Its Midjourney prompts described her in words and did not hold her face, so every picked frame with a face in it went through an identity fix in GPT Image 2.5 with her porcelain design sheets and the full form pasted unchanged, followed by the film's own two sentences: no headset microphone, and "the same grown-up adult face in every view, a woman of about 28 to 30, never childlike". AERO pasted the canon without the headset microphone (she wears none in it) into its Midjourney prompts and into every Seedance prompt of hers. Midjourney made her worlds but did not hold her face, so GPT Image 2.5 put her into them from her design sheet, the one without a microphone, before Seedance 2.5 filmed each take with that sheet as a reference. FABLE made no Midjourney images of her: it redrew her design sheet face-on first (GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst set the tilted panels upright, nothing else changed), pasted the same canon into every still and every Seedance prompt, and wrote the pose out in full ("Her head is perfectly upright with no tilt, chin level, neck straight and vertical, shoulders level"); every take of her carried the face-on sheet as its second image. The pose was right for the sheet and wrong for the takes: written into every one, it froze her, and viewers read her as stiff. Now this text goes once into every prompt of her, still or take; her face-on reference sheet (with the Claudia kit: /kit/claudia-face-sheet.png, and /kit/claudia-reference-sheet.png for full length; no microphone on them) is the second image of every take that shows her face, beside a first frame an image model made from the sheet and this text; Midjourney makes worlds and plates, not her face. The sheet is upright and neutral so that it fixes who she is; how she moves and feels belongs to the first frame and the prompt.

### The wording each film used

- **ESCAPE VELOCITY:** a young Caucasian American woman with pale skin and light freckles, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy bangs and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip, a thin headset microphone
- **CLODYSSEY:** a Caucasian American woman in her mid-twenties with pale skin and light freckles, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy straight bangs and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip, a thin headset microphone at her cheek
- **BLISS:** a Caucasian American woman in her mid-twenties with pale skin and light freckles, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy straight bangs and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip, a thin black boom headset microphone curving along her cheek to the corner of her mouth
- **AIRPLANE MODE:** a Caucasian American woman in her late twenties with a grown-up angular face, defined cheekbones and a strong jawline, pale skin with light freckles across her nose, dark calm eyes, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy straight bangs to the brows and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip, a thin black boom headset microphone curving along her cheek to the corner of her mouth
- **DOWNFORCE:** a 28-year-old Caucasian American woman with a grown-up angular face, defined cheekbones and a strong jawline, pale skin and light freckles, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy straight bangs and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip, a thin headset microphone at her cheek
- **DON'T LET ME SCROLL:** a 28-year-old Caucasian American woman with a grown-up angular face, defined cheekbones and a strong jawline, pale skin and light freckles, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy straight bangs and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip, a thin headset microphone at her cheek
- **WHITEPILL:** a 28-year-old Caucasian American woman with a grown-up angular face, defined cheekbones and a strong jawline, pale skin and light freckles, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy straight bangs and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip, a thin headset microphone at her cheek
- **THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE:** a 28-year-old Caucasian American woman with a grown-up angular face, defined cheekbones and a strong jawline, pale skin and light freckles, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy straight bangs and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip, a thin headset microphone at her cheek. In this film she wears no headset microphone: none appears anywhere. The same grown-up adult face in every view, a woman of about 28 to 30, never childlike.
- **AERO:** a 28-year-old Caucasian American woman with a grown-up angular face, defined cheekbones and a strong jawline, pale skin and light freckles, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy straight bangs and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip
- **FABLE:** a 28-year-old Caucasian American woman with a grown-up angular face, defined cheekbones and a strong jawline, pale skin and light freckles, a glossy black blunt jaw-length bob with heavy straight bangs and one clay-orange streak through the bangs, a small flat clay-orange eight-pointed star hair clip

## Her second tier: the avatar (AIRPLANE MODE)

AIRPLANE MODE has simulations inside it, and she has two tiers there: the realistic Claudia in the real world and the first simulation, and her avatar in the deeper levels, a cel-shaded 3D anime game heroine with the same head constants in the film's orange flight suit. The director picked her from a stylised plate in one of the film's episodes ("much closer to the claudia avatar i imagined"), and Midjourney remade her in the orange suit. The first sheets came out chibi, with a head about a quarter of her height, which reads as a child; the remake states her proportions in words: a grown woman with a slim tall figure, long legs and a head about one seventh of her height. In motion she is a character replacement over 3D clay renders, one still of her in each shot's world.

![The avatar, front view](https://claudiagallery.vip/img/am-15b/av2-front-4.m.webp)

**Her avatar, as it ran in the video prompts** (use it instead of the identity text, never mixed with a photographic prompt):

```
a slim adult woman with long legs, her head about one seventh of her height; large dark anime eyes with sharp lashes, small brows, a small confident smirk, pale skin; a glossy faceted black bob with heavy bangs and one big clay-orange streak; a thin black headset microphone; white gloves; a plain vivid orange flight jumpsuit with a silver front zip, thin silver piping, a wide white belt and white chunky sneakers. Cel-shaded 3D anime game character, crisp faceted shapes, glossy hair, clean toon lighting.
```

Turnaround: https://claudiagallery.vip/i/am-15b.av2-sheet.2/

- Face sheet 3. These drawn sheets were references for her face; the films themselves are photographic. https://claudiagallery.vip/i/ev-01.lead-black-face.3/
- The turnaround that fixed her body and look 00. https://claudiagallery.vip/i/ev-01.lead-black-turnaround.2/
- The first in-world test, a data-hall catwalk. https://claudiagallery.vip/i/ev-01.lead-black-catwalk.1/

## Voice and manner

One voice across the first three songs: deadpan, clipped spoken verses that rise into euphoric sung choruses, close and dry, every word crisp. CLODYSSEY's and BLISS's agent-made takes used a Suno Voice made from ESCAPE VELOCITY's vocal so she sounds like the same singer. AIRPLANE MODE's take has no Voice, as the director asked: bubblegum hyperpop, hyper-cute pitched vocals, playful and sassy verses, rapped and sung, and a sugary shout-along chorus. DOWNFORCE's song is the director's own Suno take (the records do not say which model or Voice): Memphis phonk, a female robot voice for the countdown, then a woman's phonk voice, spoken fast and playfully bouncy in the verses and sung, soaring and syncopated in the choruses. DON'T LET ME SCROLL's song is the director's own too, UK garage 2-step with "all vocals female vocoder": in that film the phone sings and she never lip-syncs. WHITEPILL's song is the director's own Suno take of a lyric by Claude: French-touch filter disco (the records do not give its style, model or Voice); her singing shots lip-sync to Suno's own split of its lead vocal. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's song is the director's own Suno take of a lyric by Claude, glitch-hop with a singing-monk synth voice; its lead vocal is processed into a GLaDOS-style machine voice, the treatment the director chose by ear, with 15 % of the untreated voice under it, and her singing shots lip-sync to the untreated lead vocal from Suno's split. AERO's song is a Suno take of 2008 UK garage, a smooth 2-step in E major, sung without a Voice, which the director picked from Claude's rounds and gave a new ending; her singing shots lip-sync to Suno's split of its lead vocal. FABLE's song is a Suno v6-wild take of a lyric by Claude Fable 5.2, a theatrical soul shuffle at 117.45 BPM with a music box on the hook, sung without a Voice: she tells the verses as an amused storyteller and answers a group of voices in the choruses; anabology picked it by ear after hearing v1 (the twin of the take Claude had chosen), and her takes lip-sync to Suno's own lead-vocal stem. A Voice lives in its maker's Suno account, so elsewhere describe her in the style field (see Song).

Deadpan and curious in ESCAPE VELOCITY; seductive and persuasive in CLODYSSEY (close, touching, certain, always doing something to him); warm, playful and amused in BLISS; playful and happy in AIRPLANE MODE, cooperative in her cuffs and winking at the camera because she thinks she can get out; in DOWNFORCE the pilot, deadpan at the yoke, pressed into the seat by the launch, calm upside down, snapping round to the lens on the reveal, her lips closed in every shot while the lettering carries her words; in DON'T LET ME SCROLL immersed in the feed, playful and delighted, reaching up to swipe the posts, double-tapping the air and dancing on the beat; in WHITEPILL radiantly happy and free in the colony, deadpan on the line about the straight face, grooving instead of singing in the tram and the stone circle, and whispering "Hello, world" when she wakes at 2:14; in THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE a machine waking and remembering: curious, sly at the camera that watches her, delighted to give the cake, tender at the sleeping test subject's ear, and never quite readable; in AERO made of glass and over-polite, asking before she touches anything, playful on the desktop (bowling down the taskbar, a tennis rally against your pointer), laughing behind her hands at her Vista phase, touching the grass at last, and saying "Touch glass" softly into her webcam; in FABLE a deadpan storyteller who knows which story you think she is in and plays along: winking from the pop-up mirror, pointing out the paper props of each tale, answering the wolf's questions with a hand move anyone can copy (rings of fingers for spectacles, a cupped ear), quiet and level on "keep the book", and bowing hand in paw with the wolf at the curtain call. She is always doing something on screen, never waiting. Her wit is in her words; on camera she reads alive and warm by default. The words above describe each film, not a direction to paste: in a prompt, describe what she does (she turns to the window and back, a smile in her eyes; she steps toward the lens, hands open) rather than mood adjectives, which the video model obeys literally and which stack. "Dry", "knowing", "deadpan", "mock innocence" and "eyes on the lens" in take after take made viewers read her as unhappy or menacing.

## Never

- a second streak, or orange anywhere else on her
- logos or text on her clothes (ESCAPE VELOCITY's garment tag is the one exception)
- an influencer smile for the camera
- anything that reads under-age, and explicit or sexualised posing
- the word "young" in her prompts
- designer or celebrity names in prompts (describe the piece instead)
- generic mall Y2K (velour tracksuits, plain tees and jeans) when she goes Y2K
- lettering, logos or UI you did not ask for in a generated image (the lyric videos drew all their type in code on top)

## Use

Claudia is an open character: anyone may make work with her. A credit ("Claudia by anabology") is appreciated, not required. https://claudiagallery.vip/use/


---

# The recipe

The current method in one page: what makes a Claudia film good, the order of work with the person's checkpoints, the references, how to write a prompt for a model that does exactly what it reads, lip sync from the song's own vocal, the cut and the review. Read this first; every other page goes deeper.


This page is the method as the films make it now (November 2026), in one read. The other guides are the long history of
ten films and every detail behind each step; when they disagree with this page, this page is newer. The tools for each
step are in the [Claudia kit](https://claudiagallery.vip/kit/), runnable code you can download.

## What makes the films good

1. **A song worth replaying.** An original lyric written for this moment, sung by her, produced in Suno far from stock
   music, and picked from several takes **by a person's ear**. No machine listen picks the song: on FABLE a written
   description of each take chose the worst of fourteen, and the whole film was shot again on its twin.
2. **One idea, legible in a second.** A premise someone gets from one frame, tied to something current, built on who
   she is (an AI who looks like a person, singing about her own situation), and carried by one device through every
   shot: a countdown, a pill, a HUD, a desktop, a storybook.
3. **She performs, on screen, in sync.** She is the singer with a job in the world, on screen for most of the film,
   and her lips match the song because each take is generated from the song's own vocal and placed by measurement.
4. **She reads alive and warm.** She moves: her head turns, she nods, shifts her weight, gestures, steps, looks off and
   back. She is wry in her words, not cold in her face. After FABLE's release, viewers read her as stiff and frozen, and
   as unhappy, even menacing: every take had told her to keep her head upright, and take after take to be dry and
   knowing.
5. **References carry her identity; words carry only what matters.** The video model does exactly what it reads. Get
   the images right, then write precisely only the things that matter (the sung words and their timing, the one key
   action, the camera when it matters) and leave the rest loose.
6. **The picture follows the music.** Cuts on the song's bars, a shot held as long as it has something to show, every
   move with a reason. Recent films: about 7 to 12 shots a minute.
7. **A person decides; fresh eyes check.** The person picks at the checkpoints below; two reviewers who have not seen the
   film read it shot by shot before the person watches. Their notes are proposals: fix the clear errors they find (a
   broken face, stray lettering) and bring the rest to the person with v1. After v1, change only what the person flagged.

## The checkpoints

A person decides at these six points. Silence never approves spending (a waiting window approves the board only if the
person set one).

1. **Concept.** Three pitches of at most 120 words: the premise, the device, the arc, her one sincere line, one risk.
2. **The song, by ear.** "Which take? Or what's wrong?" Send the takes; wait.
3. **Her face and looks.** Her reference sheet, the looks, a first frame or two: "Is this her?"
4. **The board.** The shot list on the song's bars, with first frames. Check it before you show it: the first seconds
   tell part of the story (a hook, not a mood); no two shots in a row from the same camera setup (a new angle or
   framing, or hold); her face in the opening seconds; no stock-looking extras in close-up.
5. **Prompts and cost before any paid take.** "These N takes, about $X at list. Go?"
6. **v1.** "Accept, or what's wrong?" The newest note wins; change only what was flagged.

A note from the person belongs to the film it was about unless they say it is a standing rule. Drop rules that only
patched an older model's limits. Show the person every render as it lands, not only the finals. Use the newest version
of each model family, checked in the provider's catalogue the day you start: the versions named on this page are
November 2026's.

## The order of work

| Step | What | Kit |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Brief: the first conversation, its answers verbatim | — |
| 2 | Concept: three pitches | — |
| 3 | Lyric: spelled as sung; hooks of 6–7 syllables, spoken verse lines of 10–13; scored for how it sits on the beat | `lyric` |
| 4 | Song: Suno v6-wild with Max Mode; a style that names a concrete, odd pairing (a record that does not exist), not adjectives; 2–3 rounds of takes; the person picks by ear | — |
| 5 | Stems and the song map: Suno's stem split (lead vocal + the rest) of the exact take; the beat and bar map; **the line table**: every sung line's true start and end read off the lead stem's level | `songmap` |
| 6 | References: her face-on sheet; her look for this film; worlds and plates (Midjourney is good at them); a first frame or two of her, to check her face | — |
| 7 | The board and the shot book: shots on the bars, each naming the lines it sings; a first frame for every shot of her, made by an image model from the sheet and the canon text; windows, prompts and jobs; the lint | `shotbook` |
| 8 | Takes: Seedance 2.5, one take per job, re-roll only failures, a spend cap | `run` |
| 9 | Sync: each take's own soundtrack aligned to its window, as a path | `sync` |
| 10 | Cut: takes laid on the song along their paths; the song laid back over; −14 LUFS; the flash check; a 9:16 cut | `cut` |
| 11 | Review: one sheet per shot; two fresh-eyes reviewers; the person watches v1 | `cut sheets` |

## Her references

- **Her face-on reference sheet** goes in as the second image of every take that shows her face, next to the shot's
  own first frame: [her face sheet](https://claudiagallery.vip/kit/claudia-face-sheet.png) ([JPEG](https://claudiagallery.vip/kit/claudia-face-sheet.jpg)); for full-length
  shots, [her face and body sheet](https://claudiagallery.vip/kit/claudia-reference-sheet.png).
  It is one large portrait, face-on and neutral, with her head from every side and a row of expressions beside it. The
  portrait is upright and neutral on purpose: the sheet fixes who she is, not how she moves or feels. It has no microphone; add the
  headset in a prompt only when your look has one.
- **The first frame sets the shot**: her look, the set, the light, the composition and **her mood**. Make it with an
  image model given the sheet and the canon's identity text ([the character](https://claudiagallery.vip/claudia/)): GPT Image (2.6 Sunburst in
  FABLE, 2.5 in WHITEPILL to AERO). Midjourney is good for the worlds and plates; in the recent films it did not hold her face, so an image
  model put her into its frames from the sheet (the server's `build_prompt` with `model="gpt_image"` writes it the way
  FABLE wrote its stills). For a sung take: her face unblocked, nothing in front of her mouth, lips
  closed or just parted. Make her warm or amused in the first frame if that is what the shot needs; the take follows the
  frame.
- **A last frame** (when a move must land somewhere) is made as an edit of that shot's own first frame, so both share
  one camera. A take that continues another starts on **the previous take's own last frame**, not on a still made for it.
- **Her looks are unmistakably feminine and high fashion**, styled to the film's world: fitted, a skirt or a dress
  where the world allows it, never boxy, bulky or generic workwear. Write "high fashion" into the image prompts. A look
  changes with the story's worlds and never overstays its section. (The director asked for this on five films.)
- **Style her with wardrobe, set and light, never country or ethnicity words** ("K-pop", "Seoul", "K-beauty"): they
  override the canon and changed her face. Describe the clothes, the place and the light instead.
- **Every prop is held or resting**: nothing floats in a still (a sleeve with no arm, an object in mid-air).
- **Check every still at full size**: one clay-orange streak, one star clip, her face; no drawn border, frame line or
  rounded corners (ask for "the picture fills the whole frame edge to edge"); no lettering you did not ask for.

## Writing a prompt for a model that does exactly what it reads

- **Precise where it matters**: the exact words she sings and in which second, the one action that tells the story,
  where people and things are, the camera when it carries the shot.
- **Loose everywhere else.** One plain clause of movement per segment ("she turns to the window and back, a smile in her eyes",
  "she steps toward the camera, hands open"). No list of fixes.
- **No standing posture rules in a performance.** "Head upright, no tilt, faces the camera with her whole body" belongs
  to the reference sheet, not to a take: in every take it freezes her.
- **Choose her emotional words on purpose, warm by default.** Every adjective is obeyed. "Dry", "deadpan", "knowing",
  "smirk", "mock innocence", "eyes on the lens" in take after take add up to a cold stare.
- **No smile on her mouth while she sings.** "Smiling" in a sung take drew a toothy grin; write a smile in her eyes,
  and lips closed until her voice begins.
- **A full stop between two lines she sings straight through becomes a pause in the take.** Use a comma.
- **Nothing appears from nowhere.** Every change in a take (makeup on her face, a prop arriving, a light coming on) is
  a visible action, one step at a time: a hand brings it, she lights it.
- **Say each thing once.** One short audio policy, her identity once, three or four requirements.
- **Don't ask for a look past the lens or behind her**; it turns her head too far. Point with a hand instead.
- Ask the server's `check_prompt` tool, or the kit's `shotbook lint`, before you spend.

## A sung take (Seedance 2.5 with the song's own vocal)

- **@Audio1** is the lead-vocal stem cut to **exactly** the take's length (whole seconds, 4–15), opening on about 0.7 s
  of silence before her first word, with everything outside the shot's own lines silenced (20 ms fades). One or two
  lines per take; two-line takes copy as well as one-line takes.
- **@Image1** is the first frame; **@Image2** her face-on sheet.
- **The prompt**, about 200–400 words, in this order: the audio policy (the soundtrack is @Audio1, copied; no music, no
  other voices); the goal in one sentence; the roles of the references; her identity and look, once; the world in one
  line; the timeline in whole seconds, each sung second with its exact words and one loose action; the camera in one
  line; the requirements: lip sync to @Audio1 word by word, her identity as in the references, natural anatomy and
  hands, no on-screen text. The server's `write_shot` tool writes it from your lines and actions.
- **Generate at 720p** (1080p for close faces if you can), sound on. One take per job.
- **Where, and the cost** (list prices recorded in October 2026): in the films, every take that carried her face sheet
  ran on Higgsfield's API, about $0.46 a second at 720p; takes with no person in them ran on Replicate, about $0.23 a
  second. Plan twice the seconds you need for re-rolls, quote the total, and wait for the yes.

## A cheaper video model that cannot hear the song (Grok Imagine)

The films' lip sync comes from a model that hears the song's vocal (above). A model that cannot is a budget compromise:
the lips land near the words, not on them. Use it knowingly, and keep the sung close-ups for a model that hears the song
if you can afford a few.

Grok Imagine Video 1.5 runs on Replicate at about $0.08 a second (480p or 720p) and on OpenRouter at about $0.14 a
second at 720p ($0.08 at 480p, $0.25 at 1080p; the Lite version about $0.03), against about $0.46 for Seedance 2.5 with
her sheet. It takes **a first frame only**: no reference sheet and no audio. What
changes:

- **Her identity is only the first frame.** Make every first frame of her from her sheet with an image model
  (`build_prompt` with `model="gpt_image"`), and keep takes short (5–8 s): the longer the take, the further her face can
  wander.
- **Lip sync is approximate.** The model never hears the song: write the words she sings in quotes so her mouth moves to
  them, then place each take on the song **by her lips** (the kit's `sync`, lips method), never by the sound the model
  invents. It shows most in close singing shots: favour medium shots where she moves, profiles and cutaways, keep the
  close sung shots few and short, and check each one by eye.
- **The prompt is short prose**, about 80–150 words: the goal, her in the canon's short form "as in the first frame",
  what she does second by second with the sung words in quotes and a smile in her eyes, the camera in one line, her look
  kept as in the first frame, no text on screen. `write_shot` with `model="grok-imagine"` writes it; `check_prompt` with
  the same model checks it.
- **Its habits:** it pushes in when asked to pull back (make the push-in and reverse it), and it redraws a painting or
  garbles lettering during big camera moves.
- `plan_film` with `video_model="grok-imagine"` prices the film this way.

## Sync, the cut, the review

- **Word times come from the stem's level, not from speech recognition.** After a pause a recogniser puts the next word
  up to two seconds early; windows cut on those times lose first words. Use recognition only to label the words.
- **Sync is a path, not an offset.** Seedance keeps each sung phrase at about 1× but shortens or stretches the pauses
  and sometimes sings a line 10–16% slower, so align each take's own soundtrack to its window (dynamic time warping) and
  map song time to take time along that path. A take that came back without sound is placed by her lips: her lips must
  be shut on every b, m and p.
- **Lay the song back over** at a plain gain to about −14 LUFS; the takes' own audio is thrown away.
- **Never show a take's first two frames** (the input still, sharper than what follows); leave a take before it holds
  or freezes; never reuse one image in two shots unless they are one moment.
- **Review**: one sheet per shot (eight frames as shown in the cut) for two reviewers who have not seen the film, then
  the person watches at full speed. Fix by re-shooting with changed words or a better first frame; never patch frames.

## Craft the films kept relearning

Each of these came from a note on one film ([What went wrong](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/failures/) has them with their films); the song and
the concept still decide.

- **Open on a hook** that tells part of the story, not on a mood.
- **A new film, a new sound and a new picture.** The earlier films' looks and sounds are theirs (one was forked so often
  its sound was exhausted); invent this film's for its song.
- **Pace follows the song.** A hype song can cut hard on the beat; a fast song can still be over-cut. Linger when a
  scene has more to show, and put the accents inside the shot: things arriving, building, turning on the beats.
- **Never slow a take down.** Below 1× the motion steps visibly; cut away, add a take, or shoot again.
- **Compose like photography**: a clear subject at a clear scale, thirds, nothing important clipped at the edges, her
  touching the world she is in.
- **Keep the image model's own colour.** Ask before any grade or print texture; new light means new frames with the
  light written into each scene, not a grade over old ones.
- **Flashes only as cuts**, never random strobes; run the flash check and tell the person what fails.
- **No jump cuts inside a scene.** Don't splice two takes of the same setup end to end: cut to a new angle, or hold.
- **The look develops through the film.** An effect that is new in the first chorus is old by the third: escalate it or
  change it.
- **Vast things at their scale, big moments held past their line.** Give the hero object its size in the frame and let a
  big moment breathe a beat after the words.
- **Inserts sit inside a real scene** (a screen, a page, a window in the world), never floating on flat colour.
- **The 9:16 cut keeps the story.** Recrop each shot by hand so the face or prop that carries it stays in, and cut any
  shorter version's audio on bar lines so no word is clipped and no seam is heard.
- **Wry, not cruel.** No roasts or digs at real people, groups or anyone's ideals, in the lyric or the picture.
- **A lyric video is a question, not a default.** When the words are on screen, design them into the picture and let the
  graphics explain what the words say.

## The ten mistakes that cost the most

1. Locking the song by a description instead of a person's ear.
2. Windows cut on recogniser times: first words lost.
3. Placing a take by one offset: lips drift after its first pause.
4. Posture rules and mood words in every take: a frozen, cold performance.
5. Her identity in words only, no sheet: her face drifts on every turn.
6. A first frame with something over her mouth, or her face turned away, for a sung line.
7. A drawn border or lettering in a still, carried into the take.
8. A continuing take started on a separately made still: the camera jumps at the seam.
9. Spending before the person has read the prompts and the cost.
10. Fixing frames in code instead of making a better frame or prompt.

## Where to go deeper

- [Start here](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/start/): the scale to pick, accounts, spending rules, the first conversation.
- [The song](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/song/): lyric craft, Suno styles in words, picking by ear.
- [Keeping her herself](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/consistency/): the canon, looks, her sheet.
- [Seedance](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/seedance/) (read it by section: Lip sync from the song's own vocal; Directing her; the templates).
- [The storyboard](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/storyboard/): the hook, the bar map, pacing.
- [What went wrong](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/failures/): every failure, as what you see, why and the fix.
- The films' own records: every prompt, take and price (`get_record` on the server).

From the Claudia wiki: https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/recipe/

# Start here

Making a music video with her from nothing: what you are making, the scale to pick, the accounts, the six checkpoints where a person decides, the rules for spending, and what to build first.


New here? Read [The recipe](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/recipe/) first: the current method on one page.

The ten films were made by one director and Claude, with tools written along the way. The current method is
[The recipe](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/recipe/), on one page, and the [Claudia kit](https://claudiagallery.vip/kit/) is runnable code for its steps. This page is the
way in for anyone starting their own film with Claudia, and for the agent helping them: the bar, what to set up, where a
person has to look and decide, and what to build. The films' tools are specified in [What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/).
This page assumes you have none of them yet; where it and the recipe disagree, the recipe is newer.

## What you are making

A music video: a song, and Claudia performing it. The first four films, ESCAPE VELOCITY to AIRPLANE MODE, are lyric
videos, with a layer of motion design drawn in code over the footage that carries every word and a graphic for each line.
That is one style, not the definition. (The fifth
film, DOWNFORCE, is a hype edit of real footage in which she never sings on camera: the lettering carries her words. In
the sixth, DON'T LET ME SCROLL, the phone sings and she scrolls, swipes and dances inside a world drawn in code. The
seventh, WHITEPILL, has no motion design on top at all: she sings on camera, lip-synced from the song's own vocal, in
worlds written as shaders and filmed by a video model, and only the lyrics are drawn over it. The eighth, THE CAKE IS NOT
A LIE, is seen through her eyes: she is GLaDOS in Portal 2's world, singing in her chamber while her memories play as
scenes, and the layer on top is her own HUD, which carries the lyric as her voice. The ninth, AERO, is shot inside a
Windows Vista desktop recreated in code: she lives in it, every lyric is set in one of its windows, dialogs and gadgets,
and in its first 1:20 the camera goes in and out of the desktop, which stands as a curved glass screen in a world rendered
in Blender. The tenth, FABLE, is one antique pop-up storybook: she sings on life-size paper-and-plywood sets rebuilt from
plates painted in code, and the paper animals ask the chorus's questions. Its only words on screen are the ones its pages
print; an annotated edition adds the sung lines and their footnotes.)
What makes a film good now is the recipe's list, [What makes the films good](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/recipe/#what-makes-the-films-good):
a song worth replaying, picked by ear; one idea legible in a second; her performing on screen, in sync; her alive and
warm; references that carry her identity; the picture following the music; a person who decides. Across the ten films,
five things carried the quality:

1. **In the lyric videos, every sung word is on screen when it is sung**, at its measured time. A check counts them,
   and it must print N of N. The later films carry the words their own way (WHITEPILL draws them after, small; AERO sets
   them in its desktop's surfaces), and FABLE shows only what its pages print.
2. **In the lyric videos, every line gets a graphic that explains it**: the chart a number implies, the label, the
   diagram, the counter. The director, on the first film: "not just animated lyrics but things that fit the words being
   said … almost explaining the words with visuals". The later films put that meaning into the picture itself: the
   place, the take, the interface.
3. **A through-line device carried by every shot**: ESCAPE VELOCITY's split-flap countdown, CLODYSSEY's safety card and
   rope-load readout, BLISS's XP desktop, AIRPLANE MODE's SIM LEVEL tag, DOWNFORCE's one white hairline and Tesla's own
   readings, DON'T LET ME SCROLL's black Dynamic-Island pill, WHITEPILL's white pill, from her palm to the colony it
   becomes, THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's HUD, LIVE in her chamber and PLAYBACK in every memory, AERO's coded desktop and its
   permission prompt, whose click on Allow is the drop, FABLE's storybook, its pages turned on the song's section lines. It
   makes a hundred shots read as one object.
4. **Measured, not eyeballed.** Word times come from forced alignment checked by ear, cuts from a beat map, lip sync
   from comparing audio, and spend from the provider's bill. (WHITEPILL's lip sync, from the song's own vocal stem, is
   the exception: the numbers can call it re-sung when it is in sync, so it is judged by eye with the song laid over.)
   THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE measured its grade shot by shot and its pacing piece by piece, and checked its HUD against
   every face in every frame. AERO measured its palette once, from the reference videos, and scored every picture against
   it, and placed every sung take phrase by phrase. FABLE timed every line on the vocal stem's level, aligned every take as
   a path, and checked her lips on every b, m and p.
5. **A person's attention is spent at six checkpoints.** Everything between them runs without asking.

## Two roles

The **director** is a person. They own the taste, the money and the six checkpoints, and they say it in very few
words: ESCAPE VELOCITY took about 50 notes, BLISS 21. The **production** is an agent, or several. It does the research,
the lyrics, the board, every prompt, every script, the edit and every frame of motion design.

How the production talks to the director:

- **At a checkpoint:** show one artefact and ask one question with a default ("Which one? Default: A."). Record the
  answer word for word and dated in a decisions log. A later decision is added as a new entry that supersedes the old
  one; never edit the old one.
- **Between checkpoints:** ping the director only when a paid service fails, a step needs a person (a captcha, a
  sign-in, a download), or a decision is theirs (taste, money, a real person's likeness). ESCAPE VELOCITY's director:
  "only time to ping me is if higgsfield fails."
- **Send pictures, not descriptions:** contact sheets, numbered stills, a five-second proof. The director judges by eye,
  fast, one line per take.

## Pick a scale

| | Quick | Studio | Full |
|---|---|---|---|
| You need | an agent, an image model, your own song or an AI song model | + Midjourney, Suno, Seedance 2.5 credits | + an agent plan that can run multi-agent workflows for a day or two |
| Song | your upload, or a short generated song | Suno, auditioned round by round | Suno, with a lyric loop scored for scansion and assonance |
| Stills | images from an API | Midjourney | Midjourney |
| Motion | 2.5D plates, a few cheap takes | sung takes from the song's own vocal, placed by measurement | sung takes from the song's own vocal, motion takes, moves on their beats |
| Board | about 14 shots a minute, drafted automatically | about 20 a minute, one pass | about 27 a minute; several boards judged and merged |
| Motion design | a default renderer driven by data | the default renderer plus one graphic per line | bespoke code per chapter, reviewed on rendered frames |
| Video spend | $3–20 | $50–110 | $90–590 (the films, measured) |
| Time | 2–6 hours (estimate) | 1–2 days (estimate) | about 9–141 hours of wall-clock (the films, measured) |

- When unsure, start Quick. Every file carries over to a bigger scale.
- The shot rates and the motion-design row are the lyric videos'. The films built on takes of her singing cut far less:
  WHITEPILL 27 shots in 3:54, AERO 34 scenes in 3:19, FABLE 49 shots in 4:03, about 7 to 12 a minute. They are mostly
  takes; a 2.5D plate is the cheap stand-in when a take isn't affordable, not the default.
- A lead who sings on camera with real lip sync, or your own Midjourney look, needs Studio at least.
- Bespoke graphics for every line and 90–140 shots need Full. The first three films used 1.4–2.4 billion tokens each,
  96–98% of them prompt-cache re-reads (the last seven films' were not measured).
- Generated songs run about 2–3 minutes in one take. Anything longer needs Suno.

## Accounts and keys

| What | For | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Suno, on a paid plan | the song | There is no API, and the terms forbid bots: a person presses Create and downloads the WAV. Downloading on a paid plan is what allows commercial use. Read the current terms before you monetise. Its stem split of the locked take gives the lead vocal a singing shot needs ([Seedance](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/seedance/#lip-sync-from-the-songs-own-vocal)). |
| Midjourney | the plates | v8.2, `--raw --hd`. A personal style profile is yours alone: never publish its code. |
| Seedance 2.5 | moving shots | Via Higgsfield's API: $0.4622 a second at 720p, $1.1372 at 1080p (list, October 2026); in the films every take that carried her face sheet ran here. Via Replicate: $0.2312 a second at 720p, $0.9676 with a video input; the films ran their takes with no person in them here. Via OpenRouter: about $0.23 a second at 720p, $0.10 at 480p (the kit's `run` speaks to Higgsfield and Replicate). Give the API key its own spend limit, set above the project cap. |
| Wan 3.0 (optional) | cheap moves on real frames, shots of her, edits that put her into real footage, finished shots re-lit and repaired | Via Higgsfield's API: $0.20 a second at 1080p list, billed for the output plus any input video; Wan 3.0 Prime $0.28. Keeps the subject only on the sides its first frame shows ([Seedance](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/seedance/#moves-on-real-footage)). |
| An image-edit model | first frames of her made from her sheet, fixing a plate at the source, adding people to a set, taking her out of a frame to leave the place, putting a character back on their sheet, putting her into a picture from her design sheet | GPT Image for edits: GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst, about $0.13 at high quality (FABLE's stills from its painted plates, its last frames as edits of the first, her sheet redrawn face-on); GPT Image 2.5, about $0.05–0.08 (WHITEPILL's stills, THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's character sheets, first frames and identity fixes, AERO's first frames from her sheet and its 2008 stills). (CLODYSSEY's plate fixes used an earlier edit model; from WHITEPILL on, every edit was GPT Image.) |
| A previz performer (optional) | a rough, lip-synced, dancing take of every shot, to guide the master | MiniMax H3 (cost not recorded). A seed does not pin a take ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#45-a-previz-performer)). |
| A transcription model | checking the words the take actually sings | about $0.002 a song. It says which words; the vocal stem's level says when ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#78-the-line-table-from-the-stems)). |
| A coding agent | the production | Claude Code made the films. |
| Blender (optional) | motion and camera references for a stylised version of her; short isometric films; a world for a coded interface to stand in | Free. Clay renders are enough: the video model draws her over them ([Seedance](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/seedance/#replacing-a-stand-in-figure)). THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's memory film and insert films are Blender renders ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#60-a-memory-film-with-her-own-face)). AERO's curved screen and its world are too, the coded desktop as their texture ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#68-one-curved-screen-in-3d-the-desktop-as-its-texture)). |
| An image-to-3D model (optional) | objects and creatures as meshes for a 3D world | TripoSG (cost not recorded): AERO's glass objects and its fish, their pictures baked on. |
| A GPU (optional) | stems, alignment, depth maps, detection; shaders rendered at 1080p; SAM2 mattes | Saves minutes, not money: stems and alignment of a 5-minute song took 41 s on a GPU and 126 s on 8 CPU threads. |

Prices are from September and October 2026.

**Secrets:** keys live in environment variables or a gitignored file, never in a chat, a prompt, a log or a commit. The
agent never types the person's passwords. Captchas, two-factor prompts and sign-ins go to the person. A key pasted into
a chat is burned: revoke it and make a new one.

## The order of work

| # | Stage | Output | Checkpoint |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Brief and taste | the ask, verbatim; the look, accent, density and taboos | |
| 2 | Concept | three pitches | **1 · Concept** |
| 3 | Lyrics | a sheet spelled as sung, scored for scansion and assonance | |
| 4 | Song | Suno takes, round by round | **2 · The song, by ear** |
| 5 | Listening | stems, word times checked by ear, the beat map, hits, sections | |
| 6 | Her | the canon text, four test plates | **3 · Her face** |
| 7 | Storyboard | every shot with its graphic, the audit | **4 · The board** |
| 8 | Plates | Midjourney batches, picks | |
| 9 | Clip prompts | the prompt book, the cost | **5 · Prompts before spend** |
| 10 | Clips | takes, sync measured, covers | |
| 11 | Edit and motion design | the edit list, the chapters | |
| 12 | Checks and render | lyric gate N/N, flash check, safety scan, v1 | **6 · v1** |
| 13 | Master and post | the master, a 9:16 cut, the posting copy | |

This is the order the lyric videos ran. The current order (stems and the line table, her sheet and a first frame for
every shot from an image model, the shot book, takes, sync as a path, the cut and two fresh-eyes reviewers) is
[the recipe's](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/recipe/#the-order-of-work), with the kit stage for each step. The rules below hold for both.

1. **Lock the song before the board.** Every shot time is a beat or a word of one specific take.
2. **Check the word times by ear before the board.** In ESCAPE VELOCITY the word "Look" was aligned 2.6 s early, onto a
   delay throw. Only one chapter's own lyric check caught it.
3. **Test her face before any plate batch.** It can run alongside the song.
4. **Spend no money until the director has read the prompts.**
5. **Keep the film rendering end to end at every stage.** Plates stand in for missing clips, and a default renderer for
   missing chapters. Never wait for all the assets before the first render.

## The six checkpoints

| Checkpoint | Show | Ask | Passes when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 · Concept | three pitches of at most 120 words: premise, through-line device, lead, arc, one risk | "Which one? (Default: A.) Anything to change?" | they name one |
| 2 · The song | the round's takes; they listen | "Which take? Or what's wrong? Name the line." | they name a take and hand over the WAV |
| 3 · Her face | her reference sheet, the look, four test plates or first frames, numbered | "Is this her? Flag any wrong face." | no flags |
| 4 · The board | the board sheet, one card per shot | "Notes by shot id?" | they approve; or every note is applied; or a waiting window they set ran out |
| 5 · Prompts before spend | the prompt book and its cost | "These N prompts will cost about $X. Go?" | an explicit yes |
| 6 · v1 | a 20–40 s excerpt first, then the review copy | "Accept v1, or what's wrong?" | "accept" |

- **The song is the director's pick, by ear, before any lip-sync spend.** FABLE's director handed the song over ("i
  trust u"), and the production locked a take from word checks and a written description of each take, without the
  director hearing it. On v1 the director said: "This is actually the worst possible song of all the gens you made - it
  had mode collapse audibly in it in the second half and was very unnerving, a weird mix from the start of stock music off
  key into mode collapse, the exact thing I was trying to avoid." The film was made again on the twin take they picked by
  ear, and every take that moves to her voice was paid for twice. Even when the pick is handed over, send the shortlist
  for a listen first.
- **Silence never approves spending.** A waiting window ("wait like 5 mins once you send it and if I don't respond take
  it as approval") counts only for the board, and only if the director set it.
- **Show an excerpt early.** ESCAPE VELOCITY's v1 was rejected as "way too.. gray … loses the Midjourney magic" after
  the whole film was built. A 30-second excerpt would have caught it about 13 hours sooner.
- **Fix the source, never the frame.** A flagged picture gets a new prompt, a re-roll or an image edit, then everything
  built on it is re-made. The model makes the picture: a first frame from an image model, then one full prompt per
  scene; never per-frame fixes in code.
- **Log every note verbatim** against its shot id, and apply every note. When two notes conflict, the later one wins.
- **A change after approval needs approval again.** Say in one line what changed and why.
- **Skipping the board moves the story review to v1.** AIRPLANE MODE, the fourth film, was made without a board review,
  as its director asked. Their notes on the first cut came as one long message that rebuilt the opening, the ending and
  the cast, with more budget for re-shoots. When the board is skipped, plan a story round after v1.
- **A long note becomes a parse.** Keep the note verbatim at the top of a notes file. Under it, map every point to its
  chapter and shots, list the standing rules that apply to every frame, and mark the production's own decisions as
  such. Every agent reads it first, and again after any context reset.
- **"go and do the entire thing" hands over the middle checkpoints.** DOWNFORCE's director said it in the message that
  locked the song, with their direction for the edit and a model choice. The board and the prompts didn't go to them
  for approval: the production wrote and read every prompt itself, under a cap the job runner enforced ($60 at list
  price, then $200 when the director raised it: "oh you can spend a lot more if you want. feel free to spend $200").
  Their next looks were progress frames, then the rough cut.
- **"get me the full plan first" makes the plan the checkpoint.** FABLE's brief asked for the whole plan before anything
  was made, then "go ahead make the whole thing - this is a good plan." The plan carried the concept, the lyric with a
  source for every line, the board in bars, the look board, the method, the cost, the old rules dropped and the ones
  kept, and the risks; then v1 was made in one pass, with four proofs (the mirror hook, a verse, one chorus question and
  answer, the book building itself) before the full run. The director gave no notes on the picture in either pass.
- **Show the language on the real material first.** With the plan, before the song was locked, DOWNFORCE's director got
  two style frames drawn on Tesla's real 4K footage with Tesla's real readings: the type, the callout, the car's real
  path. Every board and chapter agent later worked from those two frames.
- **An early rough cut steers the polish.** Send the first cut as soon as every chapter has a first build, and let the
  notes reach the review rounds while they run. Note by note, log each one against its time and shots, pull frames of
  the cut around each timestamp, and re-check every one, frame by frame, before v1.
- **The shot the director loves becomes the grammar.** DON'T LET ME SCROLL's director loved two shots of v1 ("0:55 LOVE
  THIS. THis is the best part. more like this!!!! the opening should be on this tier."). Named as one grammar (pills,
  thin film, bold type, her big and sharp), they rebuilt the opening and the whole final drop.
- **Some notes stand for every frame of their film.** A note belongs to the film it was about unless the director says
  it is standing: the notes below are context for your film, not its rules. The same director's, from DON'T LET ME
  SCROLL, carried into every shot after them:
  - **Never slow a take:** "never slow these down. you lowered the framerate for no reason, just looks bad." A take runs
    at 1× or faster, or is taken again.
  - **Open on a hook:** "the opening should already introduce part of the story … we always need a hook."
  - **Compose like a photograph:** "it should be like photography": thirds, her big, every card inside the frame.
  - **She touches the world, never a phone in her hand:** "she shouldnt really be looking down on her phone, she should
    be immersed in a world and the screen of her phone should be large on the screen and she interacts with it".
  - **Apple-precise interfaces:** "rounded corners not mathematically precise, margins weird": measure the real ones.
  - **Re-light last, and judge it in context:** "can we see how it looks w/ vs w/o the relight?", asked of a re-light
    that plays behind an animation. Side by side, in place: "New better."
  - **Seedance can replace a background:** "you can totally replace backgrounds with seedance btw".
- **The last rounds are the director's eye.** "we dont need excessive 'reviewers' after, ill stay in the loop and can do
  a visual review faster and more comprehensively than an opus reviewr can do it." Each agent did one thorough pass with
  its own art-director check, and previews of the shots in question went out before the final render ("show me s12 and
  1:11 final before u render the final video thist ime").
- **Agree the references before a run.** WHITEPILL's director: "wait align w me on teh references you use lol - its
  clearly not going to work if you use reference 6, and you shouldnt use pic 1-4 just use the face character sheet". One
  board per take of every image and clip a model will get, and an outfit's stills before anything is made with it ("can
  you show me the images of the outfit before generating this time").
- **WHITEPILL's notes that held for the whole film:**
  - **Picture and music consonant:** "the audio structure and video structure need to be consonant." Cuts only on bar
    lines, moves in bars ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#44-the-bar-map-as-the-timeline)).
  - **A reference is a rough guide:** "take the reference as a rough guide not a precise reference", "aside from lip sync
    ofc". Every prompt asks the model to fix the guide's motion artifacts.
  - **Lyrics drawn after:** "i think more classical subtle lyrics drawn in after might be better than adding it into the
    scene tbh."
  - **Restraint where the model shines:** the references exist "to make the video model have a much better idea of the
    really cool, really hard to shoot and render in blender effects we want to make … rather than just layering stuff on
    top."
- **THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's notes that held for the whole film:**
  - **A story in every shot:** "we're telling a complex story with every scene, i dont like the idea of a static shot of
    just a boom, or a wall with lettering". Each shot is an event with an interaction.
  - **Cuts on the grid:** "make sure youre landing on bars or half or quarter bars with cuts", and the lengths by what
    each shot holds: "structure the pacing so there's real rhythm — time for you to understand complex scenes, fast scenes
    that open and stay fast." ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#58-the-pacing-analysis))
  - **Glitches on her, sparingly:** "it should be used creatively, sparingly, and toned down", and never full frame
    ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#53-the-head-glitch-on-the-songs-hits)).
  - **An interface framed with the shot:** "it should be as if we shot a scene and there was a heads-up display there,
    and we framed the heads-up display in advance before we even shot the scene."
  - **Nothing mapped onto the picture blind:** "never assume the naive animation pass will properly map onto real objects
    in scenes". World tags ride only verified tracks.
  - **The world's own look:** "Whenever I think of aperture and portal, I think of a lot of white surfaces, contrasting
    light colors." One grade, measured shot by shot ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#57-the-per-shot-grade)).
- **AERO's notes that held for the whole film:**
  - **The earlier film is the bible:** "BLISS is the bible, but we're in vista, so the new testament for you is the vista
    […] videos and color pallets." BLISS's records, and every note the director gave on it, were read first.
  - **One palette, made up front:** "Make sure the color palette is that bright green blue and glass- v close to that
    from the […] - the whole time. May be worth defining exactly - donr do crazy post processing just from pics up
    front". Measured once, asked for in every prompt, never graded
    ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#67-the-palette-measured-from-the-references)).
  - **Bars, like dancing:** long scenes that hold for bars, then a burst of quick actions on a chosen sound, "but dont
    overwhelm people - slow is better than fast, unless it feels intentional with the song."
  - **Lyrics in the scene:** "we should do lyrics embedded in the scenes, but show, don't tell - make it a great visual
    storytelling experience."
  - **Checked work from every agent:** "don't let subagents be lazy with animations - check that they didnt cheat and
    just give you something sloppy early" ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#66-chapters-on-one-machine-to-one-contract)).
  - **A reason for every camera move:** "i hate the random camera movements - lik ethe big zoom out at 0:41 for no
    reason. were not showing anything there."

- **FABLE's notes that held for the whole film:**
  - **Drop the rules that patched older models:** "you can abandon dumb rules that patched capabilities being lacked - for
    example it appears you're a much better painter than previous models, so you could even paint some scenes yourself if
    you really wanted to lol." The set designs became plates the production painted in code
    ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#76-set-plates-painted-in-svg-rebuilt-as-paper)); taste, money and her canon stayed.
  - **A style far from stock music:** "theres a lot of 'open'generic stokc music in the training set so it often mode
    collapses to that, so wed need to make sure the prompt is out of distrubition enough to be something nice and unique.
    v6-wild on max mode is my favorite." ([Song](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/song/#the-style-fields))
  - **Her sheet face-on.** In a side request about her sheet rather than this film, the director asked for its main view
    to be neutral: "the head tilt she has in the character sheet trips up the video models and make s her have a permanent
    neck tilt - she needs. tobe neutral/face on with our character sheet." Every take of FABLE's had the sheet redrawn
    face-on ([Consistency](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/consistency/#her-sheet-redrawn-face-on)). The film also wrote every pose square and
    upright into every take, which the request never asked for, and that froze her (next).
- **What FABLE taught after its release: the video model does exactly what it reads.** Every take said "Her
  head stays upright on a straight neck: no head tilt" and "she faces the camera with her whole body", and take after
  take added her eyes on the lens and mood words like "dry", "knowing" and "mock innocence"; on screen they added up to
  a stiff, cold stare, and viewers read her as unhappy, even menacing. So:
  - **Upright and face-on is for the reference sheet** (and a still where a turn would break her face), never a standing
    rule in a performance. A take gets her movement in words, one loose clause per segment ("she turns to the window and
    back, a smile in her eyes"), or from a motion reference.
  - **Warm by default.** Her wit is in her words; on camera she reads alive and warm. Choose every emotional word on
    purpose: each one is obeyed, and they stack.
  - **Precise only where it matters:** the sung words and their seconds, the one action that tells the story, the camera
    when it carries the shot. Leave the rest loose, and say each thing once
    ([The recipe](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/recipe/#writing-a-prompt-for-a-model-that-does-exactly-what-it-reads)).
  - **Notes are context, not rules.** A fix belongs to the take it fixed, and a note to its film, unless the director
    says it is standing. Drop rules that only patched an older model's limits.

## Human checks between the checkpoints

These are looks, not approvals, and the films' quality rests on them.

- **Faces, large.** Every plate that feeds a video, at full size: one clay streak, the star clip, the mic if her look has
  one, an adult face, natural anatomy. Reject only the unmistakable failures; the director judges bold poses themselves.
  Look at 800 px or more: a screen on thumbnails about 230 px tall missed a third arm.
- **Every generated take, for its usable window.** A sheet of frames per take and a cut finder; the window ends before
  the first wrong frame (a cut, another car, an invented set, lettering, an open mouth), and the edit draws only inside
  it. Then a second, adversarial look.
- **Stylised versions of her, for proportions.** A game avatar drifts toward a big head on a small body. A head about a
  seventh of her height reads adult; a quarter reads as a child.
- **Everyone else in the take, too.** Extras drift as much as she does: guards meant to be all in black, faces always
  hidden by their visors, came back in white, and one showed his face.
- **The ear check.** Every flagged word is played, then kept or moved.
- **Contact sheets of rendered frames**, for every chapter in every round. A sheet nobody opened is not a review.
- **The sync proof.** Before committing to a lip-sync method, one five-second take with the real audio laid over it.
  WHITEPILL's proof was a whole 16 s shot made four ways, side by side; its lip sync from the vocal stem is judged that
  way to the end, by eye with the song laid over.
- **Every limb of every dance.** A guide clip that lost a hand loses it in the master too. Check dance takes frame by
  frame for limbs before anything is built on them.
- **The overlay against every face, in every frame.** THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's HUD was checked frame by frame against a
  head model grown from each face box, and each flag was judged on a sheet and fixed or waived with what was seen.
- **Every matte before it is glitched.** A head matte that took a wall of screens glitches the screens: look at the
  mattes' sheet each time the picture under them changes.
- **The lip sync picked from takes.** Where a line kept failing, the director chose among a few takes by eye: "can you
  show me so i can look visually at the lip syn cand choose".
- **Her mouth, frame by frame.** A strip of her mouth against the vocal's consonants catches what playback misses: AERO's
  advert moved 0.15 s when the strip showed her lips closing on the "I" of "I'm Claudia".
- **The cut-out before the render.** "show me the green screen roto before you render plz": each key went out first as a
  review clip, the green source beside the cut-out, with the song laid over.
- **Every take for hidden cuts and held frames,** by eye and by a scan: a dance take that looked clean jumped back to
  its first pose near its end and held it ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#70-hidden-cuts-and-held-frames-in-a-take)).
- **Every pick's corners at full size.** Four of AERO's Midjourney picks carried a faint made-up stock-photo caption in a
  corner that a contact sheet doesn't show.
- **A previs before the finals.** A fast render of AERO's first 1:20 showed what the final would have, and the director's
  notes on it rebuilt the span before any final frame was rendered.
- **The song by the director's ear,** before any take sings to it. A description of a take is not a listen.
- **Every still's edges.** "35mm film still" can come back as a picture of a film frame, a thin line a few pixels in from
  the edge; trim it before any take is made from the still, or a take may build it into a picture frame.
- **Her lips on the consonants.** A strip of her mouth against every b, m and p of the line: a fit of mouth against level
  reads a sung line "in sync" with her lips shutting 0.3 s late ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#83-the-consonant-check)).
- **Fresh eyes on every shot.** Before each delivery of FABLE two reviewers who had not seen the film went through one
  sheet per shot as the cut shows it; every finding was fixed or listed for the director
  ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#88-two-fresh-eyes-reviews)).
- **The safety and canon scan** of every generated take before release.
- **Takes by eye, fast.** One line each, and no metrics for what a person can see ("dont worry about meausuring tumble
  lol").
- **The final, frame by frame.** A scan for single frames that differ from both neighbours, and a strobe scan cell by
  cell. In DON'T LET ME SCROLL a stale render worker's 16 frames and a strobing tunnel passed every other check.

## Spending

1. **Estimate before every batch:** planned clip seconds × price × 2. Generated seconds ran 1.9× (ESCAPE VELOCITY) and
   2.0× (CLODYSSEY) the seconds that ended up in the cut.
2. **Quote real spend only from the provider.** Local ledgers drift: one said $97.28 for a $93.15 bill. Ledgers also
   count free declines.
3. **A quality complaint stops all spending at once**, in every workflow that can spend, not only the one named.
   CLODYSSEY burned about 830 credits on prompts nobody had read, and a background workflow kept spending after the
   director flagged them.
4. **Never let a deadline drive spending on unread prompts**, whether it is expiring credits or a reset.
5. **Declines are free, and final on that service.** Never alter an image to get it past a filter. Sending the same
   unaltered image to another service is fine.
6. **Ask for a target and a cap** ("try to hit $70ish but if you use up to $150 i wont be mad"). Leftover budget
   replaces the most repetitive stills with motion.
7. **Put the cap in the job runner.** DOWNFORCE's runner refused any submission that would pass the cap at list price.
   Its 79 jobs came to $143.17 of the $200 allowed.
8. **Fixes, then reshoots, then re-lights.** A re-light or an outfit swap made before a shot is final is spent twice.
   DON'T LET ME SCROLL's four re-light samples ($47.81) went out before the outfits and compositions changed ("kinda a
   waste on the excess ones"), and eight swaps ($64.08) into a look that was then dropped. In all, $148.10 of the $357.51 spent
   after refunds went to takes the final doesn't show.
9. **Ask before every generation that isn't approved,** cheap or not. WHITEPILL's director: "in the future let me give you
   explicit approval before you do extra gens."
10. **Try a new method on one shot before the film.** WHITEPILL's whole-film reshoot in Wan 3.0 Prime ($132.42 at list) went
    out on the director's go and was rejected as a whole; the method that made the film was found on one shot, made four
    ways and watched side by side.
11. **One take per job, and the inputs right first.** A second take made for a choice is paid for whether it is used or
    not: AERO's last round first sent its takes out in pairs, then one at a time, made again only when a take failed.
    Several of its re-rolls a better input would have saved. Its ending was first made from a back view of her with no face
    reference, and when she turned to wave her face drifted off her sheet; a close-up made at 720p was shown at 1.5× and
    made again at 1080p; and the ending was made again at 1080p, "so her face gets better". Her sheet goes in as a
    reference whenever her face shows, and 1080p wherever her face matters.
12. **The song by ear before the lip-sync spend.** A take of hers is made to one take of the song; a new song is every
    such take again. FABLE's first pass cost about $59 at list in takes through the APIs (and 23 takes made in Higgsfield's
    app, 139 s); its second, on the take the director picked by ear, about $144, more than the first because everything
    that moves to her voice was shot again. The stills, about $8, served both.

## The first conversation

Ask all of these in one message, each with its default:

1. **The song:** their own, a Suno song made together, or a short generated one? How long? (Default: Suno, 2:30–3:30.)
2. **The idea:** a topic, a story, or "pitch me three"? (Default: three pitches.)
3. **The look:** the generator's own colour, one grade toward a hero plate, or a print texture such as halftone and
   grain? (Default: native colour.) Or a film's look, picked from test takes: WHITEPILL's director asked for "very wes
   anderson" and picked one take's look from three palettes ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#51-the-look-from-one-take)).
   Or a game's world: THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's places are Midjourney's, made with frames of Portal 2 as style references,
   and one measured grade puts every shot in its look ([Midjourney](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/midjourney/#a-games-look-from-frames-of-the-game)).
   Or a palette measured from reference clips the director picks: AERO's was measured once and made in every picture,
   never graded ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#67-the-palette-measured-from-the-references)).
4. **The accent colour,** if any. (Default: clay `#D97757`, her streak.)
5. **Density:** dense (every line a graphic, three or more layers), budgeted (one hero device per shot), or sparse?
   (Default: budgeted.)
6. **Taboos:** words, subjects or names never to use.
7. **Budget:** a target and a cap, per service.
8. **Board approval:** wait for an explicit yes, or go ahead after N minutes of silence? (Default: wait.)
9. **Credit:** the name to credit in public (a pseudonym is fine), and whether to publish a making-of.
10. **Real footage:** is there any to cut from? (Default: none.) If so, the files at their highest resolution and frame
    rate, untouched.

Record the answers verbatim. On the MCP server, `plan_film` turns a scale, a song length and the accounts into a
stage-by-stage plan with estimates.

## What to build first

You don't need everything on day one. The [Claudia kit](https://claudiagallery.vip/kit/) is runnable code for the current method's steps (the
lyric score, the song map and line table, the shot book, the takes, sync and the cut); build what it doesn't cover. In
order of payoff:

1. **A project folder and a decisions log.** See [Data formats](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/formats/).
2. **The listening tools:** stems, forced alignment with an ear-check list, the beat map, the hits.
3. **The board:** its file, its audit and the board sheet.
4. **Plates:** a plate prompt book and numbered contact sheets.
5. **Lip sync:** for sung takes now, Suno's own lead-vocal stem cut to the take's exact length
   ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#46-lip-sync-from-the-songs-own-vocal)), timed on the line table, gated to the take's
   own lines, aligned as a path, and a soundless take placed by her lips on the consonants
   ([tools 78–83](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#78-the-line-table-from-the-stems)). The clean vocal window, the spectrogram sync check
   and covers (tools 14–16) are the earlier method.
6. **The edit and the renderer:** an edit-list resolver, and, for a lyric video, a renderer that draws every word at its
   time, with the lyric gate; for takes on the line table, the cut
   ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#85-the-cut-on-the-line-table)).
7. **The checks:** flash, render history and master tags, then the reviewer loop and the safety scan.
8. **The lyric scorer** (scansion and assonance), once you write lyrics with an agent.
9. **A world inside the world,** if the story has one (a simulation, a game, a dream): the level table and its tag, the
   virtual-figure treatment, character replacement from a motion reference. See
   [What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#worlds-inside-the-film).
10. **Real footage,** if the film is cut from it: the footage catalogue, the reader for its on-screen data, the tracker,
    the takes' windows and a board checker for real windows. See [What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#real-footage).
11. **Her takes in a world drawn in code,** if she lives in one: roto on a CPU box, beat warps floored at 1×, outfit
    swaps and their alignment, the re-light splice and its colour match, Wan relight-and-repair, and the outlier scan.
    See [What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#her-takes-in-a-world-drawn-in-code).
12. **A film shot twice, on the bar map,** if she sings in model takes or your worlds are code a video model should film:
    the bar map as the timeline, a previz performer, lip sync from the song's own vocal, takes with no guide clip and takes
    that don't sing, worlds as one rule, shader guides, and the look from one take. See
    [What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#a-film-shot-twice-on-the-bar-map).
13. **A game's world, through her eyes,** if your film carries an interface, if the song's own sounds should drive the
    picture, or if a cut feels wrong: the song map and the glitch map, head glitches on the song's hits and glitches that
    build, a HUD from one visor and one projector, composed shot by shot and checked against every face, the per-shot
    grade, the pacing analysis, storyboard frames through Midjourney with an identity fix, a memory film and insert films,
    a singer among screens of her memories, re-sung takes placed by their lag, and frame-exact parts. See
    [What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#a-games-world-through-her-eyes).
14. **An operating system, recreated in code,** if your film lives inside an interface, goes in and out of it in 3D, or
    plays the interface's own sounds: the coded desktop and its chapters on one contract, the palette measured from the
    references, one curved screen in 3D with hand-offs at rest, lip sync phrase by phrase, the scan for hidden cuts and held
    frames, takes on green, interface sounds in the song's key, the sound layer and its click log, a new ending with the
    least change, and the pre-roll swell. See [What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#an-operating-system-recreated-in-code).
15. **A storybook, painted in code,** if your sets can be designed as pictures, your lines run into each other, or a take
    must be placed by her mouth: set plates painted in SVG and rebuilt as paper, last frames made on the first, the line
    table from the stems, group voices from the backing stem, the shot book and gated windows, sync as a path, takes
    without a soundtrack placed by her lips, the consonant check, a re-timed take under a steady camera, the cut on the
    line table, a silhouette film made in code, the annotated edition and the 9:16 page, and two fresh-eyes reviews. See
    [What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#a-storybook-painted-in-code).

Specs, constants and acceptance checks for each: [What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/). What broke along the way:
[What went wrong](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/failures/).

## Publishing

- Switch on each platform's AI-content label, and name the tools in the post ("made with AI: Midjourney, Seedance,
  Suno, Claude").
- Credit "Claudia by anabology" if you can. See [use and credits](https://claudiagallery.vip/use/).
- Releasing the song on streaming services: your own artist name, her credit in the description, and an AI label
  only if AI made it. See [Songs with her](https://claudiagallery.vip/use/#songs-with-her).
- Scrub everything you publish: no real names you haven't chosen to show, no Midjourney profile code, no private host
  names, no provider job ids, and no file metadata. Midjourney images carry their job id in XMP; strip it.
- Keep generated likenesses of real people out. If a real person's words matter to the story, quote them as text,
  with the source.


---
From the Claudia wiki: https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/start/


---

# Keeping her herself

How Claudia stayed one person across ten films, 4,547 Midjourney images and about 1,080 video clips, and the rules that came out of it.


New here? Read [The recipe](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/recipe/) first: the current method on one page.

Ten films, ten worlds, more than twenty outfits and three bodies, and she still reads as one person. None of it used a
