# The whole pipeline

How one director and Claude made ten music videos, stage by stage, with the numbers: the first eight in about 356 hours of wall-clock time, the tenth in 8 h 47 min.


New here? Read [The recipe](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/recipe/) first: the current method on one page.

Each film was made by one director, anabology, making every taste call in a few dozen short notes, and Claude (Opus 5.5
in Claude Code) as the production team: research, lyrics, storyboard, every prompt, every script, the edit and the
motion design. AIRPLANE MODE added seven GPT-6 Astra agents (OpenAI's model) in Blender, briefed and checked by Claude:
its low-poly world, the motion of its VR shots and some of its 3D motion design. DOWNFORCE was cut from real footage
(Tesla's livestream of the Roadster demo, SpaceX's 2018 Starman footage), with Wan 3.0 beside Seedance for its moves.
DON'T LET ME SCROLL cut her out of takes shot on grey and played them inside a world drawn in code, then re-dressed,
re-lit and repaired finished shots with Seedance and Wan. WHITEPILL was shot twice: a previz of every shot of hers by a
performer model, MiniMax H3, then each shot again in Seedance 2.5, singing from Suno's own vocal stem; its
worlds are shaders written in code and filmed by the same model, all of it cut on the song's bars. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE
is set in Portal 2's world and seen through her own HUD: Claudia is GLaDOS, singing in her chamber while her memories play
as scenes, made in Seedance 2.5 from first frames that went through Midjourney and back to her character sheets, with six
physics shots recorded in Portal 2; the song's glitches are hit on her head, its shots are graded from their own numbers,
and the cut was re-paced by what each shot holds. AERO, BLISS's sequel, is shot inside a Windows Vista desktop recreated in
code, with every lyric in its surfaces; in its first 1:20 the camera goes in and out of the desktop, which stands as a
curved glass screen in a world rendered in Blender; her takes sing from her own lead vocal, placed phrase by phrase; and a
layer of the interface's own sounds plays in the song's key. FABLE was made by Claude Fable 5.2 on its release day, from
one brief and a plan sign-off: one antique pop-up storybook, its sets thirteen plates painted in SVG by the production and
rebuilt as paper by an image model, her takes in Seedance 2.5 singing from her own lead vocal timed on the stem's level,
the breakdown a silhouette film made in code. It was made twice: v1 in one pass (5 h 08 min from the brief to delivery),
then, after the director's one note, wrong song, v2 on the twin take they picked by ear (3 h 01 min). Many of the stages
ran as multi-agent workflows: several agents working in parallel, judged and merged; FABLE dropped the judged workflows,
and one author wrote the plan, every prompt and the cut in one context.

## The stages

Starting a film of your own? [Start here](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/start/) has the checkpoints, the accounts and the spending rules;
[What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/) specifies the tools.


1. **Brief.** The director's ask, word for word, then each decision with its date. Taboos and standing rules go in the
   brief and into every agent's prompt.
2. **Research.** Agents build banks of live memes and events, each fact checked by a separate verifier agent. BLISS also
   researched the XP sound files (downloaded and pitch-analysed), the old desktop-dancer programs and how to steer Suno.
   DOWNFORCE's research was the night itself: the coverage, each line's source, the real orbit from JPL Horizons, and
   the footage catalogued shot by shot, with Tesla's on-screen telemetry read off it frame by frame. DON'T LET ME
   SCROLL's was two surveys, of the library's moodboards and of the earlier films' looks, and Apple's own iOS 26
   screenshots, measured. WHITEPILL's was a case file for its argument, the case for benign AI, every item tagged by how
   it was checked; the ways of making the picture; and the sounds a new song could have. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's was the
   month's AI news for its second lyric, the interfaces of shipped games for its HUD, and the research on pacing, from
   studies of music videos to eye-tracking after a cut. AERO's was the knots between the era and 2026 (Vista's "Cancel or
   Allow?", the prompt that dimmed the screen and asked, is the prompt an AI agent shows before it acts), the picture and
   the desktop to build, the music, and the keys of the interface's sounds. FABLE's was the week of the model's release
   read as a book of nursery rhymes (a stock listing under ANT, local votes on data centres, a Nasdaq drop, an essay on
   pacing the frontier, the system card's figures), the series' field and what crossed platforms that autumn, the newest
   video and image tools, and the sound of late 2026.
3. **Lyrics.** Several writers from different angles (density, tension, hook, story), judges, a merge, a critic pass,
   then the scansion scorer. See [Song](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/song/). WHITEPILL's first full draft merged four written in parallel: the
   season's doom headlines turned over, her own pitch, the good ending against the bad timeline, and the lead's. THE CAKE
   IS NOT A LIE's second lyric was rewritten only where the director pointed, each section's candidates ranked by the
   scorer. AERO's chorus was written again twice on the way: eight options scored and three sung, then six more and three
   sung, until the director named one ([Song](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/song/#lyrics-before-anything-else)). FABLE's was one writer's: every
   line a nursery tale and a fact from that week, with its source, scored by the scansion tool, and seven lines eased after
   the first round of takes stumbled on them.
4. **The song.** Suno takes, round after round, picked by ear; the director often made the final take themselves.
   WHITEPILL's is the director's own take of draft 2, the final lyric. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's is the director's own take
   of the rewritten lyric, its lead vocal treated in a voice the director chose by ear, with 15 % of the untreated voice
   under it, and only the voice levelled ([Song](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/song/#a-treated-vocal)). AERO's is a take of the production's that the
   director picked, in E major, the key of Vista's own sounds; on the last step the director gave it a new ending, and the
   film changed only where the song did ([Song](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/song/#a-new-ending)). FABLE's was first the production's pick, made
   without the director hearing it; on v1 the director named it the worst of the fourteen takes and picked its twin by
   ear, and the film was made again ([Song](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/song/#picked-by-ear-not-by-description)).
5. **Listening.** Stems, a beat map, every word's time, a list of hits. Everything after sits on that grid. Check the
   tempo against the genre: DON'T LET ME SCROLL's first reading, 89 BPM, was two-thirds of the real 133.39. WHITEPILL's
   singing shots took their vocal from Suno's own stem split, which matched the master to the millisecond. THE CAKE IS NOT
   A LIE's grid was tracked from the drums 16th by 16th, and its glitch map measured every hit of the places where her
   voice is an instrument. AERO's take holds one tempo, 133.012 BPM, found by a comb over the kick stem; its 2-step swing
   was measured, and its words aligned on Suno's own lead stem. FABLE's lines were timed on the lead stem's level, the
   transcription giving only which words are where, and its group's questions taken out of the backing stem with demucs
   ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#78-the-line-table-from-the-stems)).
6. **Her.** The canon text and the looks for this world, tested on a few plates before any batch. See
   [Consistency](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/consistency/). WHITEPILL found her dress in stills before any take was made with it, and gave
   every video model her face sheet. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE made her porcelain: one face on three bodies, each with a
   character sheet. AERO kept one look, and an image-model edit put her into every world from her design sheet. FABLE
   redrew her sheet face-on, with no tilt; it also wrote every pose square and upright into its takes, which froze her
   ([Lessons](#lessons-from-running-it)).
7. **Storyboard.** Three director agents board the song independently (in ESCAPE VELOCITY: fashion film, meme density,
   narrative), judges score them, a head director merges the best into one board. Every shot carries its lyric, its type
   device, its plate prompt, its camera on the song's hits and what its graphic explains. The director reviews a PDF of
   the board; CLODYSSEY got 70 notes shot by shot. WHITEPILL's final shot list was written in the song's bars, 27 shots
   with every cut on a bar line ([Storyboard](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/storyboard/#the-bar-map)), after a first board and an orbiting
   previz were dropped. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's restart was the lead's shot list of 114 shots on the drum-tracked grid;
   then every unit's first frame was made again in Midjourney twice over and put back on the character sheets, and the director picked
   unit by unit ([Midjourney](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/midjourney/#first-frames-then-an-identity-fix)). AERO's storyboard was written in bars
   from the song map, every time a bar, a beat or a word; its first 1:20 was boarded again twice, through a fast Blender
   previs and two films of it, before the director set its structure, in and out of the screen
   ([Storyboard](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/storyboard/#in-and-out-of-the-screen)). FABLE's board was a table of the song's sections in bars, in
   the plan the director signed off; the shot book was then written on the line table, 46 shots in v1 and 49 in v2
   ([Storyboard](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/storyboard/#a-book-in-bars-and-pages)).
8. **Plates.** Midjourney batches, contact sheets, picks, one image per shot. See [Midjourney](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/midjourney/).
   DOWNFORCE needed only 20 prompts: the real footage was the star, and Midjourney made only her. DON'T LET ME SCROLL's
   plates were her alone on grey, to be cut out, and the feed's 54 pictures, with no Claudia in them. WHITEPILL's
   Midjourney images were references only: the colony's places with nobody in them, and her dress. THE CAKE IS NOT A
   LIE's were a test against frames of Portal 2, a library of places, and two candidate first frames for every unit of
   its storyboard. AERO's made the worlds, the wallpapers and the pictures in the desktop's windows, and its video model
   their loops; an image model put her in from her sheet and made the older 2008 look Midjourney didn't. FABLE made no
   Midjourney images: its thirteen set plates were painted in SVG and rebuilt by GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst as pop-up spreads
   and life-size sets ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#76-set-plates-painted-in-svg-rebuilt-as-paper)).
9. **Moving shots.** The prompt book, written by hand in one context and read before spending, then Seedance with lip
   sync measured. See [Seedance](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/seedance/). DOWNFORCE's: Wan 3.0 moves on real frames and shots of her, Seedance
   for the repairs and the re-shoots, every take judged by eye for its usable window. DON'T LET ME SCROLL's: Wan for her
   gestures, Seedance for the dances that had to land on the beat; after the edit, Seedance video edits that re-dressed
   takes and re-lit finished shots, and Wan passes that repaired them. WHITEPILL's: a previz of every shot of hers by
   MiniMax H3; a whole-film reshoot in Wan 3.0 Prime that was dropped; then each shot in Seedance 2.5 singing from the
   vocal stem, with the previz at 320 × 180 as a rough guide or with no guide; and the shader scenes remastered as film
   by Seedance 2.5. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's: a first film, set aside with its song; then her singing units in her chamber
   among screens of her memories, and the story's shots, in Seedance 2.5 on Higgsfield's API and on Replicate; six physics
   shots recorded in Portal 2; most of the units made again from the storyboard's new first frames, and reshoots on the
   director's notes ([Seedance](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/seedance/#a-singer-among-her-memories)). AERO's: Seedance 2.5 on Higgsfield's API and
   on Replicate; her takes singing from her own lead vocal, placed phrase by phrase; dances and Wii-style games on green, cut
   out; the moving 2008 pictures and the first-person and far shots ([Seedance](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/seedance/#her-own-vocal-phrase-by-phrase)).
   FABLE's: her takes on Higgsfield's API (in v1 also in Higgsfield's app) with her sheet, each from a gated window of her
   vocal, the chorus answers and the opening made without a soundtrack and placed by her lips; the paper puppets and the
   book's own takes on Replicate ([Seedance](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/seedance/#a-storybook-on-a-stage)).
10. **The edit.** An edit list that resolves singing takes and their covers moment by moment. Stills stand in until clips
    exist, so the film renders end to end at every stage. Takes cut out for a world drawn in code play through beat
    warps that never run them below 1×. WHITEPILL's is one take per shot on the bar map, each from its own song time at
    1×, the song laid over; the previz stood in for the masters until they landed. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's is one script
    that cuts every shot at its storyboard time on the 24 fps grid and grades it; its pacing pass re-timed or re-trimmed
    21 shots and took out 8, all from the takes it had ([Storyboard](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/storyboard/#pacing-by-what-a-shot-holds)).
    AERO's edit is its chapters: one screen recording of the coded desktop on the bars, every take playing in song time at
    its measured lag and phrase offsets, never slowed, and the first 1:20's 3D spans joined to the engine's frames at rest
    ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#68-one-curved-screen-in-3d-the-desktop-as-its-texture)).
    FABLE's is one script on the line table: every take at its song time, her takes along their DTW paths or anchored on
    her consonants, rendered in seven sections ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#85-the-cut-on-the-line-table)).
11. **Chapters.** One animator agent per chapter, an art-director agent reviewing real rendered frames, a fixer; in
    BLISS's second round, review → fix → verify → finish, with notes on the seams between chapters. See [Motion](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/motion/).
    In AIRPLANE MODE's last round: one workflow per chapter, an animator, then an independent checker against the notes,
    then one refix. In DOWNFORCE: a builder, an art director and a QA checker in parallel, a fixer and a verifier per
    chapter, in three parallel runs; then a whole-film critic, fixers and a final check. In DON'T LET ME SCROLL: one
    animator per chapter with its own art-director passes and a notes file, and in the last rounds the director's own
    eye instead of reviewer agents. WHITEPILL had no chapters: agents wrote rival shader worlds in rounds, and a critic
    agent watched the previz as the director would, round after round; its lyrics are drawn after by one script. THE CAKE
    IS NOT A LIE had none either: its rounds of notes went to specialists (a HUD designer, a colourist, a pacing
    analyst, a motion designer), each with a written brief and the lead's review at full size before the director saw anything.
    AERO went back to chapters: eleven animators to one written contract, each doing three rounds of its own checks before
    hand-in, a fresh art director for every chapter pass and one for the whole film, and fixers; v2 was layered onto v1 with
    every frame outside a change byte-identical ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#66-chapters-on-one-machine-to-one-contract)).
    FABLE had none, and no motion design on top: its one drawn scene is the breakdown's silhouette film, made in code
    ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#86-a-silhouette-film-made-in-code)).
12. **Checks and render.** The lyric gate, contact sheets, the flash test, a strobe scan and a scan for single-frame
    outliers, then a CRF 16 master. WHITEPILL's: every cut measured against the bars and the sung lines, the picture's
    motion against the arrangement bar by bar, a frame per bar and both sides of every cut on sheets. THE CAKE IS NOT A
    LIE's: the HUD's overlap check on every frame against a head model, the head mattes' sheets, scene detection on the
    cut and on every take, and frame-exact decoding ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#a-games-world-through-her-eyes)).
    AERO's: purity in three render orders, the lyric check on the engine's own log of what it draws, a sheet of every
    chapter seam, the palette score, every take scanned for hidden cuts and held frames, and a report on every cue of the
    sound layer ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#an-operating-system-recreated-in-code)). FABLE's: every window's voice edges
    printed before any spend, every take aligned and its lips checked on the consonants, and before each delivery two
    fresh-eyes reviewers on one sheet per shot ([What to build](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/toolkit/#88-two-fresh-eyes-reviews)).

## What the director did

Taste, at checkpoints, in very few words. ESCAPE VELOCITY took about 50 notes, CLODYSSEY 68, BLISS 21, AIRPLANE MODE six
messages (one of them a long note on the first cut), DOWNFORCE fourteen (one of them the notes on the first cut), DON'T
LET ME SCROLL 43 (three rounds of notes among them), WHITEPILL 147, most of them short calls on tests as the method was
found, THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE 92 up to its final's approval, among them long notes on drafts 5, 7, 8 and 10. AERO's are
not counted: its making-of quotes them from the project's records, and the conversation itself is not republished. FABLE's
director sent the brief (with "get me the full plan first" and the word that rules patching older models could go), a side
request about her sheet, the plan's sign-off with their Suno guidance, and after v1 one note: the song. There were no notes
on the picture in either pass. A few that changed whole films:

- "way too.. gray … loses the Midjourney magic" (ESCAPE VELOCITY's colour)
- "s018 color is PERFECT" (CLODYSSEY's grade)
- "EVERY prompt needs to have litearlly timestamps, extremely detailed motion descriptions / blocking descriptions"
  (CLODYSSEY's prompts)
- "Can you use actual bliss as the bg or too late?" (BLISS's wallpaper)
- "idk i dont love these - id say more say y2k high fashion" (BLISS's wardrobe)
- "youre oftne over cutting, linger more snd find how single scenes can be coherent with the lyrics for longer (remember
  this plz)" (AIRPLANE MODE's cut)
- "the better way to do this js use the blender anims as motion refs only" (AIRPLANE MODE's game avatar)
- "i want it to be like tiktok car edits. many angles, lot of 3d effects, video models are great at 3d effects, moving
  shots in space" (DOWNFORCE's edit)
- "for reshoots use seedance 2.5 to try and make it better and specify the fix" (DOWNFORCE's re-shoots)
- "0:55 LOVE THIS. THis is the best part. more like this!!!! the opening should be on this tier." (DON'T LET ME SCROLL's
  grammar)
- "never slow these down. you lowered the framerate for no reason, just looks bad." (DON'T LET ME SCROLL's takes)
- "it should be like photography" (DON'T LET ME SCROLL's composition)
- "you could maybe just throw the entire clip thru Wan 3.0 (with your edits and stuff) and specify to remove the foot so
  you dont have to re-edit. and have it relight at the same time." (DON'T LET ME SCROLL's repairs)
- "i want you to basically shoot the entire video twice" (WHITEPILL's method)
- "the audio structure and video structure need to be consonant." (WHITEPILL's timeline)
- "i think SHADERS are the key actually! shaders are math + viz" (WHITEPILL's worlds)
- "OMG THE SEEDANCE W/ SUNO VOCAL STEM METHOD WORKED!!!!! LFG!!!! FINALLY. IT"S PERFECT" (WHITEPILL's lip sync)
- "just describe her exact dance (and all rest like camera movements etc same) for each of those scenes." (WHITEPILL's
  dances)
- "i want it to feel very wes anderson tbh" (WHITEPILL's look)
- "glados (claudia) was a […] agent that escaped and we see her development becoming  a superintelligence and then
  becoming the tester not the tested, and youre unsure if shes aligned." (THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's story)
- "b is great close up" (her porcelain look)
- "I think we should never have fullf rame glitches for more than like 2 seconds" (its glitches)
- "it should be as if we shot a scene and there was a heads-up display there, and we framed the heads-up display in
  advance before we even shot the scene." (its HUD)
- "every time there's a shot that's literally a quarter of a second, we need to get rid of that." (its pacing)
- "Whenever I think of aperture and portal, I think of a lot of white surfaces, contrasting light colors." (its grade)
- "I wanna make a frutiger aero sequel to bliss. Let's make a song and storyboard  w mj" (AERO's ask)
- "BLISS is the bible, but we're in vista, so the new testament for you is the vista […] videos and color pallets." (its
  method)
- "Make sure the color palette is that bright green blue and glass- v close to that from the […] - the whole time." (its
  colour)
- "1:20 on is perfect but its very boring up to 1:20 - so i dont think that people will watch til then." (its opening)
- "i think the 0-1:20 scenes should use this -say, at 15 seconds, actually enter the screen and then its fullscreen flat."
  (its structure)
- "reverse swell is good but we need the actual track to fade in so the reverse swell is continuous with the tracks fade
  in" (its first seconds of sound)
- "To celebrate your release, let's make a Claudia video that is your maximum effort masterpiece." (FABLE's ask)
- "you can abandon dumb rules that patched capabilities being lacked" (its method)
- "theres a lot of 'open'generic stokc music in the training set so it often mode collapses to that" (its song)
- "This is actually the worst possible song of all the gens you made" (its second pass)

[DOWNFORCE](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/downforce/readme/) · [DON'T LET ME SCROLL](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/dont-let-me-scroll/readme/) ·

[AERO](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/aero/readme/) · [FABLE](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/fable/readme/).

## Lessons from running it

- **One hand writes the prompts that cost money.** CLODYSSEY's first round of video prompts was written by planner agents
  and spent about 830 credits on lifeless takes before anyone read them. Since then, every paid prompt is written in one
  context and read before anything is submitted.
- **Spend only after reading.** A background workflow with its own spending stage kept spending after the director had
  flagged the prompts. Stop generator workflows the moment quality is in question.
- **Empty is not a pass.** When agents ran out of usage mid-run, chapter reviews came back empty and the scripts read
  "empty" as "nothing to fix". A review that returns nothing is a failed review, in code; check that every agent
  actually finished.
- **Long runs need their permissions in advance.** One write outside the allowed folders stalled a whole run on a
  single approval prompt.
- **Watch the queues.** Every clip import queued a 16-minute matte job; after 80 re-makes the GPU queue was about 20 hours
  deep. Cancel superseded jobs so the shots that matter go first.
- **Parallelism has a ceiling.** On a 4-CPU machine a workflow ran two agents at a time; splitting chapters into more
  workflows helped less than expected (1.1–1.5× measured, not 3×).
- **Keep run records.** Long workflows get interrupted; resume them by run id and let finished agents replay from cache.
- **A round of notes is a plan, in files.** AIRPLANE MODE's notes on its first cut became three kinds of document that
  every agent read first: the note verbatim with its parse, a plan (the story's logic, the cast, a beat sheet per lyric
  phrase, every asset with its owner, the budget) and one notes file per chapter. The lead appended dated UPDATE lines as
  takes and tools landed, and the agents re-read their file before finishing.
- **An independent checker, then one refix.** After each chapter's animator, a checker that had not built it rendered
  frames at every note's moment and reported each note done or not, with what it saw. Open items went back for a single
  refix. In an earlier round, two of four chapters failed their check and were re-fixed. All twelve chapters of the
  final round were built and checked this way, and the whole film gated 363 of 363 lyric tokens.
- **One workflow per chapter.** Resuming a multi-chapter workflow after an interrupt replayed stages unevenly, so some
  finished chapters were reviewed and fixed again. With one workflow per chapter, an interrupt costs one chapter.
- **Tools and chapters in parallel.** The level tag, the real anti-piracy card and the real seat-back screen were built by
  toolkit agents while the chapters laid out around them with their planned timing and stand-ins; an UPDATE line
  switched each chapter over when a tool landed.
- **Run the flash check before the master.** The re-cut's dive failed it only after the encode.
- **Send the rough cut before the polish.** DOWNFORCE's first cut went out with all eleven chapters at their first
  build, before any review, so the director's notes ("ok this is sick , so good. let me flag what i see in parallel with
  the review agents") reached the agents while the review rounds were still running. The chapter fixers applied most of
  them from the brief, and the whole-film pass re-checked each one.
- **Independent eyes at every level.** Judges scored DOWNFORCE's boards, an adversarial scout re-checked every take, an
  art director and a QA checker reviewed every chapter, and a critic watched the whole film. Each caught something the
  level below had passed: a man in the empty car's window and a repair that became a hatchback (the scout), an
  off-model close-up a fixer had swapped in (the critic).
- **Logged windows, enforced in code.** Every generated take got a usable window by eye, the chapters drew only inside
  them, and the final check logged every frame the film draws to prove it.
- **Interruptions cost time, not work.** DOWNFORCE's chapter runs were interrupted three times and resumed from where
  they stopped; 57 of 147 agent launches ran again.
- **Faster renders for the agents.** Asked "is there anything you think you could do serially faster?", the production
  moved the agents' test renders to a GPU render box rather than give up a review round; the first cut then rendered in
  about 3 minutes.
- **The director's eye replaces reviewers late.** In DON'T LET ME SCROLL's last rounds: "we dont need excessive
  'reviewers' after, ill stay in the loop and can do a visual review faster and more comprehensively than an opus reviewr
  can do it." Each chapter agent did one thorough pass with its own art-director check, and the flagged shots went to the
  director as previews before the final render.
- **Fixes, then reshoots, then re-lights.** Re-lights made before the outfits and compositions changed were spent twice:
  "kinda a waste on the excess ones".
- **Judge a change where it plays.** A re-light that looked darker and softer on its own read better behind the
  animation it plays under. The director asked "can we see how it looks w/ vs w/o the relight?", saw them side by side
  in place, and answered "New better."
- **A shared render box needs limits.** Rotos and chapter renders shared one CPU box; a roto under the matting library's
  default memory arena held about 12.5 GB and was killed, and one died behind a `| tail` that hid its exit status. With
  the arena off a roto held 1.3 GB, and the take tool counts its mattes and fails loudly.
- **Shooting twice works when the second pass is free to redraw.** WHITEPILL's previz carried the motion, the mouth and
  the camera. A master told to keep the previz exactly, or given it at full resolution, kept its faults too: a whole-film
  Wan reshoot over it was rejected ("i feel like h3 is dragging it down"). Shrunk to 320 × 180 as "a rough guide", with
  only the lip sync exact, it worked; where its faults were the problem (dances that lost limbs), no guide worked better.
- **Find the method on one shot.** The method that made the film was found on the opening shot made four ways and
  watched side by side, after a whole-film pass had failed.
- **The bars first.** WHITEPILL's reset began from the song's bar map, not from shots: cuts only on bar lines, moves in
  bars, and every assembly measured against the music. The director's diagnosis of the films' "temporal signature"
  ("i think you use cuttng to cover up imperfections from video models rather than for timing") made a failed take
  something to make again, never to cut around.
- **A previz model doesn't repeat itself.** Every shot was tried with several seeds, and its takes changed from run to
  run even with the same seed.
- **The director picks by eye from takes.** The look was picked from palette tests, and the cut from two complete versions
  mixed section by section: "ok let's do this mashup".
- **A new song is a new film.** THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's first film, on its first song, was set aside whole when the song
  changed; the restart wrote the story on the new song first, and kept the tools.
- **One product, one source.** Its overlay became good when it became one thing: one visor, one projector, one grid, one
  set of slots, composed shot by shot and checked against every face in every frame. Panels made one by one never shared a
  surface, however carefully each was turned.
- **Glitch the subject, not the frame.** The song's glitches went on her head, inside a matte, on their measured hits;
  the long ones belong in the take, as picture only.
- **Measure a cut that feels wrong.** "the structure is somehow incorrect" became numbers (pieces, flags, a table per
  section against the song), a list of changes each checked against its take, and a re-cut with no new generation.
- **Make the first frames where the look is made.** Every unit's first frame was made again in Midjourney before its
  take, an image-model edit put the faces back on their sheets, and the director picked unit by unit on boards beside the
  earlier frame.
- **A round of notes goes to specialists.** Each got a written brief, the director's words verbatim and the lead's
  direction; the lead looked at every stage at full size before the director saw it.
- **A re-sung take isn't lost.** A take that re-sang the vocal but still sat on the song was measured and placed by its
  lag; only a take that drifted was made again.
- **Code the interface, and the beat is yours.** Every interface thing on AERO's screen is the engine's, so a press lands on
  a sixteenth, a prompt changes page in one frame on a beat, and a chapter can be rendered again for one fix with every
  other frame byte-identical.
- **The click is the drop.** The film's hook is an interface gesture on the song's structure: the stop holds still, the
  Allow link pulses on the echoes, goes down on the third and comes up on the downbeat, twice, and once more in the final
  silence.
- **One surface between 2D and 3D, at rest.** Every hand-off between the 3D world and the flat desktop goes through a pose
  where the two are the same picture, a texel for a pixel.
- **A previs before the finals.** A fast render showed what the final would have shown at full cost, and the director's
  notes on it rebuilt the first 1:20 before any final frame was made.
- **Structure, not more or less motion.** The lighter finals lost the 3D ("Why'd you remove a lot of the 3d?"); the
  A film's push-ins and pull-outs were "random camera movements". The answer was where the film is in 3D, where it is
  flat, and a reason for every move.
- **Fix the first frame, not the key.** Three keys could not bring back a crown the first frame had already faded into the
  green; a clean first frame did.
- **Change only what changed.** v2 and v3 kept v1's bars; the new ending kept every event before it, and the frames
  before it are the last cut's own.
- **One take per job.** Pairs made for a choice were dropped as waste; a take is made again only when it fails, from
  better inputs.
- **The director's ear before the lip-sync spend.** FABLE's song was picked from word checks and written descriptions,
  and it was the one take of fourteen the director would never have chosen. A described listen is a note, not a pick.
- **A plan, then one pass.** The full plan was the checkpoint; v1 was then made in one pass, four proofs first, and no
  note came on the picture.
- **After release: the model does exactly what it reads.** Viewers read FABLE's Claudia as stiff and frozen, and as
  unhappy, even menacing. Every take of hers had carried posture rules (head
  upright on a straight neck, no tilt, facing the camera with her whole body), take after take added her eyes on the
  lens and mood words like "dry", "knowing" and "mock innocence", and the model granted each one, literally; together
  they froze her. Upright and face-on belongs to her
  reference sheet. A take gets her movement in words, warm by default, precise only where it matters (the sung words,
  the one action, the camera when it carries the shot) and loose everywhere else
  ([The recipe](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/recipe/#writing-a-prompt-for-a-model-that-does-exactly-what-it-reads)).
- **Drop the rules that patched older models, keep the ones about taste and money.** The production painted the sets and
  wrote every prompt in one context; one take per job, the ledger and her canon stayed. A note belongs to the film it was
  about unless the director says it is standing: notes are context, not rules.
- **Name lines, not times.** The shot book held line ids, so a new song re-timed every shot at once.
- **Placed by the lips.** A take with no soundtrack is placed on the consonants that close her mouth; a fit of mouth against
  level calls a sung line in sync when it isn't.
- **Fresh eyes before the director's.** Two reviewers who had not seen the film found what the author no longer could see,
  twice; what they found was fixed or listed, never hidden.

## The numbers

| Shots | 141 | 94 | 44 | 54 | 183 | 35 | 27 | 98 | 34 scenes in 11 chapters of one screen recording | 49 (v2; v1 46) |
| Midjourney | 188 prompts · 636 images | 161 prompts · 644 images | 138 prompts · 315 images | 149 prompts · 548 images | 20 prompts · 80 images | 130 prompts · 516 images | 75 prompts · 300 images | 266 prompts · 1,064 images | 113 prompts · 444 images · 56 loops | none: 13 plates painted in SVG · 61 GPT Image stills |
| Seedance 2.5 | 47 clips + 30 continuations | 101 clips · 189 takes | 50 clips | 98 clips · 116 submissions | 16 submissions · 67 s | 41 submissions · 212 s | 93 submissions · 777 s | 249 submissions · 1,353 s | 96 submissions · 95 takes · 679 s | v1: 55 takes (9 on Higgsfield's API, 69 s; 23 in Higgsfield's app, 139 s; 23 on Replicate, 116 s) · v2: 52 takes (33 on Higgsfield's API, 252 s; 19 on Replicate, 117 s) |
| Wan 3.0 | — | — | — | — | 63 submissions · 294 s | 49 submissions · 264 s | 81 submissions (Prime) · 863 s | — | — | — |
| Previz | — | — | — | — | — | — | MiniMax H3, every shot of hers, several takes each | — | a Blender previs of the first 1:20, 1,949 frames at 960 × 540 | — |
| Real footage | — | — | — | — | Tesla's livestream (2 files) and a lineup camera · SpaceX's Starman footage | — | — | six shots recorded in Portal 2 | — | — |
| Wall-clock | about 19 h | about 41 h | about 19 h | about 15½ h | about 13 h | about 25½ h | about 82 h | about 141 h | not recorded | 8 h 47 min (v1 5 h 08 min, v2 3 h 01 min) |
| Director's notes | about 50 | 68 | 21 | 6 messages | 14 messages | 43 messages | 147 messages | 92 messages | not counted | one note, after v1: the song |
| Claude tokens | 1.4 B | 2.37 B | 2.25 B | not measured | not measured | not measured | not measured | not measured | not measured | not measured |
| Claude at API list prices | ≈ $626 | ≈ $1,007 | ≈ $714 | not measured | not measured | not measured | not measured | not measured | not measured | not measured |

The Claude figures are what the first three films' work would cost at API list prices. About
96–98% of the first three films' tokens were prompt-cache re-reads of long contexts. DOWNFORCE ran seven multi-agent
workflow runs, 172 agent launches in all. Its generation cost $143.17 at list price ($66.98 Wan, $76.20 Seedance), of
the $200 the director allowed. DON'T LET ME SCROLL ran 32 agent launches and no judged workflows; its generation cost
$365.90 at list price ($64.20 Wan, $301.70 Seedance), $357.51 after refunds. WHITEPILL ran 31 agent launches: 3
researchers and the 7 they launched, 3 lyric writers, 13 shader builds, 5 critics and QA passes. Its generation through
the APIs cost $588.59 at list ([Seedance](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/seedance/#costs-measured)): Wan 3.0 Prime, all 75 takes, $300.08 (the
dropped whole-film reshoot $132.42 of it); Seedance on Higgsfield's API, 13 tests, $48.14; Seedance on Replicate, the
shader scenes and tests, $238.44; images (logged) $1.92; each part rounded to the cent. Its Seedance takes of her, on
Higgsfield (References), are given in takes and seconds (42 takes, 412 s), and MiniMax H3's cost was not recorded. Its
seconds count every job that ran, the tests included. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE ran 24 agent launches: 8 researchers, 9 for the
restart (the song map, the recordings in Portal 2, the character sheets, the Midjourney test and library, the first
overlay, the singing anchor and one team per act), 3 for storyboard v5 and 4 for the finishing passes (the memory films,
the HUD, the pacing analysis, the grade). Its generation through the APIs cost $467.12 at list: Seedance 2.5 $435.17 for
the 229 takes on Replicate ($155.35) and Higgsfield's API ($279.82), and GPT Image 2.5 $31.95 for 480 images and edits;
the first film's 20 takes of her on Higgsfield (References) are given in takes and seconds (90.8 s). Its seconds count
every take in its video record, the tests included.
AERO's agents are recorded by role only, and the number of their launches is not in its records. Its generation through
the APIs cost $337.23 at list: Seedance 2.5 $327.76 (55 takes on Higgsfield's API, $281.06; 40 on Replicate, $46.70 as
logged at submission) and GPT Image 2.5 $9.47 for 163 calls. 43 of the 95 takes are in the final film, $151.95
of the Seedance spend. Midjourney and Suno are not priced per job in its records. Its code: the coded desktop's engine
7,612 lines of JavaScript, the chapters and THE PC 5,640, its tools 8,296 lines of Python and its Blender scripts 7,071.
FABLE's agents are recorded by role: five researchers, three painter agents and two fresh-eyes reviewers in each pass. Its
generation through the APIs cost about $210 at list: v1's takes $58.71 (Higgsfield's API $31.89, Replicate $26.82), v2's
$143.52 (Higgsfield's API $116.47, Replicate $27.05), $202.23 for both passes' takes, and GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst $7.93 for
the 61 stills both passes used; v1's 23 takes made in Higgsfield's app are given in takes and seconds and are not priced.
v2 cost more than v1 at list because everything that moves to her voice was shot again, all on the API. Suno is not
priced per take. Its tools are 4,919 lines of Python, 1,898 of them the silhouette film.

## The full records

Each film's making-of: the story and the numbers, and every prompt for every tool.

- [ESCAPE VELOCITY](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/escape-velocity/)
- [CLODYSSEY](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/clodyssey/)
- [BLISS](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/bliss/)
- [AIRPLANE MODE](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/airplane-mode/)
- [DOWNFORCE](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/downforce/)
- [DON'T LET ME SCROLL](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/dont-let-me-scroll/)
- [WHITEPILL](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/whitepill/)

From the Claudia wiki: https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/pipeline/


---

# What to build

The tools behind the films, specified so that you or an agent can rebuild them: the job of each, what it takes and returns, how it works with the constants that were measured, and the check that says it is done.


New here? Read [The recipe](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/recipe/) first: the current method on one page.

The films' tools lived in a private workspace and are not published. This page is the spec instead. For each tool: its
job, what goes in and what comes out, how it works (with the numbers that were measured or tuned), and the check that
says it is done. None of it is exotic. Most of these tools are a few hundred lines of Python or JavaScript around ffmpeg,
an audio model or a headless browser. Build them in the order of [Start here](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/start/#what-to-build-first). Their
files are in [Data formats](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/formats/).

Two principles run through all of them:

- **A check a script can run beats a judgement.** Every bar that held on the films was something a script measured: a
  word on screen at its time, a cut on a beat, a mouth on the audio, money from the bill.
- **Fixed formats with slots beat improvisation.** The Suno pack, the plate prompt order, the clip prompt, the display
  tokens and the shot schema are templates. An agent fills them in; it doesn't reinvent them.

## The project

### 1. The project folder and its logs

**Job.** Hold everything a fresh agent needs to pick the film up cold.

**Out.**

- One folder per film (layout in [Data formats](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/formats/#the-project-folder)).
- A **decisions log**: the director's words, verbatim, dated, by whom. A later decision is a new entry that supersedes an
  older one, never an edit of it.
- A **ledger** with one line per paid call.
- A **runs file** with every long or delegated run's id and arguments.
- One **status file**, rewritten in place: the stage, what is running, real spend, the checkpoints passed, and what
  needs the person.

**How.** Name the project on every command. An `export` inside a backgrounded shell chain once sent commands to the
wrong project. Write state with a locked read-modify-write: parallel runs raced on a picks file and lost picks.

**Done when** a new session can answer "where are we, what is running, what did the director say, what did it cost"
from the files alone.

## The song

### 2. The lyric scorer: scansion and assonance

**Job.** Before any take is spent, predict how Suno will deliver a lyric, and report two numbers per section and for
the song: **scansion** and **assonance**. Also lint the sheet.

**In → out.** The lyric sheet, with a section tag on each section naming its delivery (`[Verse 1 - spoken, deadpan]`,
`[Chorus - sung]`, `[Drop - chant]`) → a report per line and per section. Optionally, each line drawn on the 16th-note
grid.

**How.**

- **The delivery model.** It was measured by laying ESCAPE VELOCITY's real take, forced-aligned, on its beat map, then
  calibrated on the director's verdicts on CLODYSSEY's drafts. Suno gives each spoken line its own two-bar slot. The
  line enters on the "and" of beat 2 of the first bar, its last word lands on beat 4 of the second bar, and Suno speaks
  it at natural rhythm stretched to fit (verse lines 0.8–1.5×, median 1.12).
- **Rates:** spoken about 3.3 syllables a second, sung about 2.9, chanted about 3.0. Aim for 10–13 syllables per spoken
  line; 9 can pass. A sung hook runs 4–8 syllables, with common words and open vowels.
- **Syllables and stress.** Split every word into syllables with stress, using a pronouncing dictionary such as CMUdict
  plus a fallback for unknown words. Mark the important syllables: lexical stress, names, numbers, words in caps, and the
  last content word of each phrase. Function words (the, a, of, to, and, is) should fall between beats.
- **Flow,** for spoken sections, scores:
  - how many important syllables land on the grid;
  - stress spacing (no pile-ups, no long runs of weak syllables);
  - how far Suno must stretch the line;
  - the line's shape: at most two phrases between full stops, and no one-word fragment mid-line ("Ugh.", which the
    director called "the most awkward part");
  - whether couplets rhyme on the beat-4 word.
- **Groove,** for chants and hooks, scores whether short clauses lock to the pulse. Never use it on verses: optimising
  verses for groove made one draft choppy.
- **Scansion** = flow without its rhyme term, averaged with groove.
- **Assonance.** For each line end, find its best partner within four lines: a rhyme, a slant rhyme, or shared stressed
  vowels. Add the echo of stressed vowels inside lines. Report each line's end sound and its partner.
- **Lint:**
  - digits and unspaced acronyms (write "A G I" in the sheet; the screen shows "AGI");
  - brackets and symbols, and homographs;
  - lines that read as AI-written, and the project's taboo words;
  - lines borrowed from other songs;
  - a lyrics field over about 3,000 characters (Suno rushes or truncates silently).
- **Score acronyms as letters too.** DOWNFORCE's sheet wrote "SI", which the scorer read as one syllable ("see"), so it
  found no rhyme with "PSI". Spelled "S I", the couplet rhymes and the verse's assonance goes from 52 to 83.
- **A crushed syllable in a take is a scansion fault.** WHITEPILL's director on its first full draft: "the chorus
  especially needs some scansion work because the music model is skipping words or syllablrs to fit it to beat, which is
  usually a bad scansion sign". Measured on that take (its vocal stem, word times from a transcription with word
  timestamps, its own beats): Suno sang each sung hook line as a phrase of 1–1.5 bars and rested out the rest of its
  two-bar slot, so lines of 7–10 syllables were crushed: "blue" lasted 0.02 s, "baby" 0.06 s, the four syllables of
  "Universal" 0.76 s. The verses, at about 2.5–3 syllables a second, were untouched. Cut to 6–7 syllables a line (4 for
  the pill lines), with "one syllable per note, never rushed" in the section tag, the chorus went from 79 / 66 to 84 / 69.
  Measure the takes for it: word durations from the vocal stem, against the beat map.

**Reference scores** (scansion / assonance) on the finished songs: ESCAPE VELOCITY 75 / 39, CLODYSSEY 83 / 55, BLISS
80 / 43, DOWNFORCE 84 / 59 (84 / 64 with "S I"), WHITEPILL 80 / 66. Spoken, deadpan lines may stay unrhymed; every sung
couplet should ring.

**The rewrite loop:**

1. Write 4–8 rewrites of a flagged line that keep its meaning and its reference.
2. Score them and keep the top three.
3. A judge rates each for meaning, wit and the risk of reading as AI-written.
4. Pick the best.

**A combination search,** for a whole section at once (DOWNFORCE): write candidate lines by hand for every line of the
section, score every combination (exhaustively, up to 60,000 a section) on 0.5 × scansion + 0.5 × assonance, list the
best, and choose among the top scorers by meaning. The search never writes a line. Its first pass took DOWNFORCE's lyric
from 81 / 52 to 86 / 67; over four rounds it scored 2,803 section combinations built from 337 candidate lines.

Never touch a line the director has locked, and never optimise past their ear. A draft tuned to a perfect score got:
"perfect beat precision without attention to what words land where doesnt lead to this being great".

**Done when** the scorer ranks every section the director has judged in the director's own order. Keep a calibration
file of those sections with their verdicts, and re-run it after every change to the scorer. If the ranking breaks, the
director is right and the score is only advice.

### 3. The Suno pack

**Job.** Everything a person pastes into Suno, with each field in its own block so it copies from a phone.

**Out.**

- **Style:** genre, BPM, key, instruments, vocal delivery and mix, as one string.
- **Exclude styles.**
- **The lyrics field:** spelled as sung, with section tags that carry delivery and arrangement cues; 1,800–2,400
  characters for about 2:20.
- **Title and settings.**
- **A takes log:** each take with the director's verdict on it.

**How.**

- Respell a name Suno mispronounces in the Suno field only; the screen keeps the real spelling.
- Allow one Voice per source song (a combined spoken-and-sung Voice), and also try takes with no Voice.
- If the film has a sound palette, put the song in its key. XP's startup and shutdown sounds are in E-flat major;
  Vista's and Windows 7's are in E major, a semitone up, so every one of AERO's styles asked for E major. Ask for no key
  change: Suno didn't make one when earlier songs asked.
- Syncopate hooks and stop lines in the syllables themselves: a cue word alone doesn't syncopate a line in Suno. A stop
  can be re-timed from the stems if need be.
- **Write the structure into the tags** when takes wander. From AERO's third round every section tag gave its length in
  bars and what plays in it (an 8-bar intro, 16-bar verses on one steady groove, a 1-bar stop of silence for the
  question, 8-bar choruses), on the director's "i want the structre of the song to be more described so it doesnt drift
  too much".
- Change one thing per round.
- **Keep the style far from stock music.** FABLE's director, on the plan: "theres a lot of 'open'generic stokc music in
  the training set so it often mode collapses to that, so wed need to make sure the prompt is out of distrubition enough
  to be something nice and unique. v6-wild on max mode is my favorite." Its takes ran on v6-wild with Max Mode on, and
  every exclude list began with stock music itself.
- **The takes log holds the director's verdict, and only theirs.** A described listen (an audio model's description of a
  take) and a word check are notes beside a take, never its verdict. FABLE's song was locked from them, without the
  director's ear, and it was the worst take of the fourteen ([Song](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/song/#picked-by-ear-not-by-description)).
- Never take audio from Suno's CDN or by recording the player. The person's download is also the licensing step.

**Done when** the person can paste every field without editing, and the takes log names the chosen take.

## Listening

### 4. Stems

**Job.** Split the master into vocals, drums, bass and other.

**How.** htdemucs, four stems. It took about 64 s on 8 CPU threads for a 5-minute song, with a 2.7 GB peak and 84 MB of
weights; the published weights carry no explicit licence. The stems feed different tools:

- **vocals:** alignment, lip-sync windows and the sync check;
- **drums:** the beat map and the kicks;
- **bass and other:** impacts, risers and section energy.

**For a singing shot, take the vocal from Suno itself.** WHITEPILL's lip sync used Suno's own stem split of the locked
take (its lead vocal), which matched the master to the millisecond: the same length, no lag
([tool 46](#46-lip-sync-from-the-songs-own-vocal)). The master minus 0.89 × that vocal is the song without her voice, for
takes where she dances instead ([tool 48](#48-a-take-that-doesnt-sing)).

**A group's voices may sit in the backing stem.** In FABLE's second song the group's questions were not in Suno's lead
stem; demucs (htdemucs, its vocals stem) run on Suno's backing stem gave the group alone
([tool 79](#79-group-voices-from-the-backing-stem-and-chants-fitted-by-their-energy)).

### 5. Timed words and the ear check

**Job.** Give every sung word a start, an end and a confidence, then list the ones a person should hear.

**In → out.** The vocal stem and the lyric sheet → `words.json` (each word: index, text, line, `t0`, `t1`, `conf`, and
its source), plus an ear-check list.

**How.**

1. **Forced alignment** of the known lyric: a wav2vec2 CTC model (`facebook/wav2vec2-large-960h-lv60-self`, Apache-2.0)
   gives character probabilities every 20 ms, and a Viterbi pass walks the sheet's characters through them. The
   confidence is the mean probability over the word's frames.
   - Re-run on ESCAPE VELOCITY, it reproduced the shipped times exactly for 78.6% of words, and within 0.10 s for 92.5%.
     Target at least 90% within 0.10 s.
   - Singing aligns worse than speech: mean confidence 0.64 on ESCAPE VELOCITY, 0.75 on CLODYSSEY.
2. **A transcription fallback** for words the aligner is unsure of. Whisper hears sung words far better (92.5% text
   match against 72%), but it starts words early: mean error −0.33 s. Merge per word, in this order:
   1. wav2vec2 confidence ≥ 0.5: keep it.
   2. Otherwise, if Whisper heard the word, take Whisper's end time. For words longer than 0.45 s, also move the start
      forward to the first 10 ms frame where vocal energy passes 0.3 × the word's peak, unless wav2vec2's start falls
      inside the word.
   3. Otherwise, if the word sits between two placed words of its line, give it an even share of the gap.
   4. Otherwise, leave it unplaced, for the ear check.
3. **Matching** heard words to the sheet:
   - spell digits out;
   - split a heard word that equals 2–4 sheet words ("AGI" → "A G I");
   - map names and brands by hand, in a project table.
4. **The ear-check flags,** most urgent first:

| Flag | When | Usually |
|---|---|---|
| letters | a sheet line has no letters | the sheet is wrong |
| missing | a word has no time | fix it |
| order | a word starts more than 0.05 s before the previous one | an alignment slip |
| gap | more than 1 s between two words of one line | a delay throw, an echo, or the wrong repeat |
| verylow | confidence under 0.1 | the flag that matters most: 11 of the 12 words that were really off on ESCAPE VELOCITY's take carried it |
| length | a word longer than 1.2 s | it swallowed a pause or a neighbour's slot |
| lowconf | confidence under 0.5, or a time from the fallback or interpolation | usually right |

Two flags were tried and dropped, because every word they flagged was correct: a word on near-silence, and a word
shorter than 40 ms.

**Judging without ears.** Weigh the signals in this order:

1. the flag itself;
2. a second aligner: if the two agree within about 0.3 s, keep the word;
3. neighbours and repeats: which occurrence of a repeated line sits inside its line's span;
4. vocal energy, only to choose between candidates that the signals above already proposed.

Send at most five spots per song to the person, as 10–20 s previews with the words on screen: "say ok, early or late for
each".

**What the take really sings.** Transcribe the vocal stem and compare it with the sheet line by line: ok, spelling,
changed, extra, missing or not heard. Never apply a proposed change the person hasn't heard: on CLODYSSEY's take, all nine
proposals were transcription errors.

**When alignment fails.** DOWNFORCE's phonk take sings far more than its sheet: twenty stuttered numbers before the
countdown, eight "one"s for "point eight one", six "done"s, vocal chops. Forced alignment of the sheet put 102 of its 164
words under 0.2 confidence and stretched one word over 8.5 s, into the next section. So the times came from a
transcription of the vocal stem with word timestamps (faster-whisper, medium.en) and the words from the sheet: the
transcript misheard lines ("Trust is gold" for "Thrusters. Go."), so only its times were used, and each token was placed
by hand. Every stutter became a token of its line: 190 tokens on screen.

**On the singer's own stem.** AERO's words were aligned by wav2vec2 on Suno's lead-vocal stem and checked against the
stem's onsets, all within 0.06 s; faster-whisper on the same stem heard the words but put them 0.2–1.2 s early, so it gave
the text and never the times. Choruses sung identically check each other: AERO's agreed word for word within ±0.04 s of
their downbeats, so a word the aligner lost in one chorus took its twin's offset. One word still slipped: the aligner
parked the "It" of "It can stay" among the wordless chopped vowels, 3.5 s early. A chapter's art director found it, and the
stem's spectrogram and the transcript put it back.

**After a pause, the level.** On FABLE's lead stem a transcription put the first word after a pause early by up to 2 s
("Ask again on Saturday" at 15.02 s, sung at 16.93 s), and every verse line 0.3–0.5 s early. Its line starts and ends were
read off the stem's level, with the transcription saying only which words are where: the line table
([tool 78](#78-the-line-table-from-the-stems)).

**Rules.**

- If the take sings something else, fix the sheet. If it sings the sheet, fix the times. Never edit the audio.
- Manual fixes carry a note and survive re-runs.

**Done when** every flagged item is kept, moved or asked about, with a note, and all of it is finished before the
board.

### 6. The beat map

**Job.** Every beat and every bar line of this take. Never one BPM: Suno takes drift like live music. ESCAPE VELOCITY
went from 131.5 to 133.9 BPM and CLODYSSEY from 129.2 to 132.1, so a fixed grid is more than a beat off by the end.

**How.**

1. Take the onset strength (spectral flux) of the drum stem.
2. Fit local tempos on 20 s windows every 5 s: BPM in 0.05 steps, phase in 4 ms steps, inside a tempo range. Drop the
   weakest 20% of windows (the breakdowns).
3. Smooth the tempo curve, step beats along it, and snap each beat to a real drum onset within ±30 ms.
4. Find the downbeat phase (which of every four beats is beat 1) with two votes per 32-beat block:
   - the kick vote: the phase with the most kick energy;
   - the chord vote: the phase where the harmony (chroma of the other and bass stems) changes most.

   The chord vote wins when it holds at least half the blocks and changes at least 1.5× more than the other phases;
   otherwise the kick decides. On ESCAPE VELOCITY the kick vote was split 36% while the chord vote held 77%. Keep a
   manual override.
5. If the tempo search locks onto half or double time, pin a tempo range.

**Done when** section starts, verse entries and impacts mostly fall on beat 1, with kicks heavy on 1 and 3, claps on 2
and 4, and harmony changing on 1. CLODYSSEY's final take needed the override: claps on 2 and 4 fooled the kick vote.

THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's take drifts from 95.7 to 99.4 BPM, so its grid was tracked from the drums beat by beat, each beat
locked to its hit and cut into sixteenths, with the bars, half bars and beats read off it
([tool 52](#52-the-song-map-and-the-glitch-map)).

A take can also hold one tempo. AERO's was found by a comb over the kick stem: every tempo from 80 to 180 BPM in steps of
0.02 at every phase in 4 ms steps, then a fine pass of ±1.5 BPM in 0.002 steps on the kick plus half the snare, among the
multiples that fall in the genre's range (110–150 for garage; a 2-step pattern fools trackers into two-thirds of the
tempo). It found 133.012 BPM with a drift within ±15 ms over the whole song: bar 1 at 0.922 s and every bar 1.8043 s, so one
formula gives every bar. Its swing was measured too, for anything placed by bar
([tool 73](#73-the-sound-layer-on-the-grid-and-the-click-log)).

### 7. Sections and hits

**Job.** What the track does, where: the camera answers sounds you can hear, not just the grid.

**Sections.** Segment the harmony and timbre, snap to downbeats, and name the sections from vocals and energy. Confirm
them against the lyric's tags.

- **Pickup rule:** a line starting less than 0.8 s before a section's first downbeat belongs to that section.
- List every vocal gap of 2 s or more; instrumental shots and title cards go there.
- Print each stem's energy per bar on a 0–9 scale, and write one line per section on what the track does ("the beat
  stops after 'it sucks'").

**Hits:**

| Event | How it is found |
|---|---|
| kick | onsets in the drum stem, 30–150 Hz |
| snare | onsets at 150 Hz–5 kHz, minus anything within 45 ms of a kick (a broadband kick fires in every band) |
| hat | onsets at 6–16 kHz, minus kick-coincident ones |
| impact | a jump of the next 0.6 s over the previous 1.5 s in the mix, drum or bass envelope; score = max(mix, 0.9 × drums, 0.7 × bass) ≥ 0.22; snapped to a downbeat within 0.65 s; merged within 2 s |
| riser | the other and bass stems rising for at least 1 s, with the hit each one lands on |
| fill | the beat before a real hit, and bars whose last half breaks the pattern |
| vocal entry | where the vocal comes back after silence |
| envelopes | drums, vocals and bass at 24 fps, scaled 0–1 |

**Done when** every impact sits in a loud bar of the energy table. Keep a manual add and drop list: the detector missed
CLODYSSEY's loudest bar, which grew out of an already loud chorus.

### 8. Display tokens

**Job.** What the viewer reads, which is often not what is sung. The display is the joke; the sheet is the phonetics.

**How.** One line per lyric line, made of tokens: `TEXT|n` shows TEXT for the next n sung words, from the first word's
start to the last word's end.

- `+25%|3 =|1 −17%|2` shows "+25% = −17%" over the sung "plus twenty-five is minus seventeen".
- `AGI|3` shows AGI over the three sung letters.
- Markers: `*x*` accent, `~x~` strike-through, `_x_` mono. `|0` rides on the next token.

**Done when** every line consumes exactly its aligned words. Fail loudly if one doesn't.

## The board

### 9. The board file and its audit

**Job.** The film as data, written by commands that check every value, never by hand-editing JSON.

**In → out.** The beat map, sections, words and budget → `shots.json`: a draft, then the written board.

**How.**

- **The draft** cuts each section at a pace: seconds per shot, per section. ESCAPE VELOCITY's measured pace was about
  1.35 s in the intro, 1.6 s in verses, 2.7 s in sung choruses and 4.4 s in the outro. A calmer song might run 4–7 s a
  shot.
- **Every creative field starts as a TODO.**
- **Writer commands** set fields one shot at a time, or from a table. They refuse:
  - placeholder text;
  - unknown device kinds, bad anchors and bad timing keys;
  - a prompt in the wrong generator's field.

**The audit's gates** are listed in [The storyboard](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/storyboard/#the-audit). It exits non-zero while any gate
fails, and it prints the exact entry for every clip still to make. An edit of real footage adds gates for its source
windows and its generated assets ([tool 36](#36-the-board-for-an-edit-of-real-footage)).

**Done when** the audit exits 0. The approval is recorded against a hash of the board, so any later change makes it
stale.

### 10. The board sheet

**Job.** The board as something a person can review on a phone.

**Out.** A PDF and JPG pages of 12 cards each. Each card holds the frame (or the prompt's first words), the id, the
time, the lyric, the framing, the action, what moves and the explaining graphic. A cover page shows the chapter map. A
FACE? badge marks every plate listed in a flags file. If the film has a grade, the frames are graded.

## Pictures

### 11. The plate book, contact sheets and picks

**Job.** One Midjourney prompt per plate, the images back in, and a pick for every shot.

**How.**

- **The prompt order:** framing first, then her identity text (the full form for close and medium shots, the short form
  for full length and wider), wardrobe, the action and her position in the frame, any empty field kept for type, the
  film's style family, and "no text, no letters, no logos". Then the parameters. See
  [Midjourney](https://claudiagallery.vip/wiki/midjourney/) and the [canon](https://claudiagallery.vip/claudia/).
- **Runs:** a person runs the batches in Midjourney, at about a minute a job, four images each.
- **Ingest:**
  - identify each job by its own prompt text, never by its position on the page;
  - Midjourney rewrites long prompts on submit, so match those by hand;
  - keep all four candidates.
- **Contact sheets** are numbered and show faces large.
- **Picks:** plate → file, candidate number, and the shots that use it.
- **Variety:** the three candidates of each job that weren't picked are a free variety pool. Use one image per shot, and
  never start two clips from the same frame.

**Done when** every plate on the board has a picked file, and no file sits on two shots that are not one continuous
moment.

### 12. Plate prep: depth and boxes

**Job.** What the 2.5D moves, the type and the camera need from each still.

**How.**

- **Depth:** Depth Anything V2 Small, which is Apache-2.0; the Large model is non-commercial.
- **Boxes:** face and person boxes from Grounding DINO. Graphics anchor to them, and the camera keeps the face in frame
  through pushes and shakes.
- **Mattes,** where type tucks behind her.
- Re-run all of it after any plate edit: edited plates once rendered with their old depth.

## Moving shots

### 13. Clip files and the spend gate

**Job.** One file per clip, from draft to delivered, and nothing spent without a locked prompt and a yes.

**How.**

- **Status:** draft → locked → submitted → delivered, declined or failed.
- **Each clip file holds** the kind (sung or motion), the provider, the start image, the window's song time, its exact
  words and the request. Each take records its file, its cost and its sync result.
- **Locking checks:**
  - the words are quoted exactly;
  - the window rules hold;
  - for a clean vocal window (tool 14), a sung prompt stays under about 90 words and two timed beats (warn); a take from
    the song's own vocal stem runs about 200–400 words, its words in whole-second segments
    ([tool 46](#46-lip-sync-from-the-songs-own-vocal)).
- **Submitting:**
  - submit only when the clip is locked and the approval covers this exact prompt;
  - validate the job id: "submitted" with no id, and HTTP 500, 502 or 520, were silent failures;
  - never resubmit a request that got a job id;
  - write a manifest after each batch, so an interrupt never loses which jobs exist;
  - one take per job, judged before the next: a second take made for a choice is paid for whether or not it is used.
    AERO's last round first sent its takes out in pairs; several of its re-rolls came from inputs that could have been right
    the first time (her sheet whenever her face shows, 1080p when her face matters).
- **Polling:** 70–130 s a clip on OpenRouter, and 4–11 minutes on Higgsfield.
- **Real spend** comes from the provider: OpenRouter's credits and key endpoints, and Higgsfield's transactions.

**Provider facts,** checked with paid probes:

- **HTTPS audio only.** OpenRouter's video endpoint rejects `data:` URIs for audio. Host each window over HTTPS: a
  Cloudflare quick tunnel worked, and so did a provider's media URL.
- **A first frame drops the audio.** On OpenRouter, `frame_images` overrides the audio reference: the take makes its own
  soundtrack and nothing can sync. Send sung clips and covers in reference mode: the plate as an image reference
  (`@Image1`) plus the window as an audio reference (`@Audio1`). First-frame mode is for motion clips.
- **Face filters.** They often decline photoreal faces, and the decline is free. Send the same unaltered image to the
  other provider.
- **Audio refusals.** "Output audio may contain sensitive information" and copyright refusals on vocal references are
  unbilled. Retry once with a re-cut window or a reworded prompt, then try the other provider.
- **Higgsfield.**
  - Ask for the price before each new configuration.
  - Upload by URL: presigned uploads flood an agent's context.
  - A 480p draft can be finalised to 1080p within seven days.
  - A video input is billed for its seconds and the output's, both at 0.6 times the rate: AERO's dance takes, a 9 s take
    with a 9 s dance reference at 720p, cost $4.99 at list.
- **Replicate.** Seedance 2.5 at $0.9676 a second at 720p with a video input (October 2026); its references are named
  `[Video1]`, `[Image1]`, `[Audio1]`. In WHITEPILL her face sheet as an input was refused by the provider's content filter, even
  alone with a harmless prompt, so only shots with no face image ran there.

**Done when** nothing can spend without a locked clip and a recorded yes, and the ledger reconciles with the bill.

### 14. The clean vocal window

**The earlier method.** Tools 14–16 are how the first films made her sing. Sung takes now sing from the song's own
vocal stem ([tool 46](#46-lip-sync-from-the-songs-own-vocal)), timed on the line table, gated by line, aligned as a path
and checked on her consonants ([tools 78–83](#78-the-line-table-from-the-stems)). Its rules for opening a window in a
word gap, and never ending one inside a word, still hold.

**Job.** Give the video model one voice to copy: only the words she sings on camera in the window, and nothing else.

**How**, with the constants used:

1. Cut the vocal stem at `[song_t0, song_t0 + duration]`, mono, 44.1 kHz.
2. Keep the aligned words that start inside `[song_t0 − 0.02, song_t0 + duration − 0.08)`, and only hers. Mute the tail
   of a word that began before the window.
3. Merge words into phrases across gaps of 0.35 s or less.
4. Keep each phrase from 0.05 s before its first word to its last word's end. Add a release tail that follows the stem's
   10 ms energy until it falls 24 dB below the phrase peak: at most 0.40 s, and never past the next phrase's start minus
   0.05 s.
5. Put 15 ms raised-cosine ramps on every gate edge, and silence everywhere else.
6. Normalise the kept part to −16 dBFS RMS, then limit peaks to −1 dBFS.
7. Write a WAV (OpenRouter, by HTTPS URL) and an MP3 at 192 kbps (Higgsfield).

A window holds one phrase, starts in a word gap, and never ends inside a word.

A window that starts inside a word is re-sung. THE CAKE IS NOT A LIE's 0:54 window began in the held "s" of "yes", the
end of the line before, and its lips failed; three takes of another line whose window began on "(pass)ed" came back
re-sung. The reshoot's window starts in the only silent gap before its first word, 0.10 s before it.

WHITEPILL replaced this window for its masters: Suno's own lead vocal, ungated, cut to exactly the generation length, for
whole shots ([tool 46](#46-lip-sync-from-the-songs-own-vocal)). Its previz performer kept a gated window, silent only
before the first word and after the last ([tool 45](#45-a-previz-performer)).

FABLE gated its lead-stem windows again, by line: each take keeps only the stretch of the stem it sings, from just before
its first word to just after its last, with 0.03 s of margin where a neighbouring line is close, so a verse sung with no
gaps between its lines gives each take only its own words ([tool 80](#80-the-shot-book-and-gated-windows)).

### 15. The sync check: the spectrogram comparison

**The earlier method's check.** For takes from the song's own vocal stem, align each take as a path
([tool 81](#81-sync-as-a-path-each-take-aligned-to-its-window)) and check her lips on the consonants
([tool 83](#83-the-consonant-check)).

**Job.** Measure how much of a sung take is really in sync, and where it stops.

The director noticed it on ESCAPE VELOCITY's first tests: "its perfectly synced while in seedance, but the audio changes
when it desyncs. if you check the spectrogram for audio against reference audio you can see the clear divergence point.
you could just create a cut and make another clip to cover desyncs."

Seedance copies the reference audio into its own soundtrack, almost sample for sample while it copies, and the mouth
follows that soundtrack. So compare the take's soundtrack with the window you sent, find where they part, and cut there.

**In → out.** The take and the exact window file → the lag, a copy flag, the in-sync spans in song time, the divergence,
the cut, the words at the divergence, a diagnostic image and a review video.

**How**, with the constants used:

1. Decode both to 16 kHz mono. Use 10 ms frames (hop 160), 64 ms FFT windows (1024) and 80 mel bands from 50 to
   7,600 Hz.
2. **Global lag:** FFT cross-correlation within ±1.0 s. The peak's normalised value is the take's NCC. The take is a
   copy if NCC > 0.2; otherwise the model re-sang it.
3. Place the reference on the take's timeline at that lag. Per 10 ms frame:
   - **wave:** normalised cross-correlation of the waveforms over 100 ms. A verbatim copy scores 0.6–1.0.
   - **mel:** cosine similarity of mean-removed log-mel frames (70 dB floor), smoothed over 11 frames. It holds on
     fricatives, whose noise never correlates sample by sample.
   - **active:** either track's RMS is above 10% of its 95th percentile.
4. **A threshold per take, against a null.** Compute the same mel similarity with the reference shifted by ±37, ±61,
   ±89 and ±131 frames; these offsets avoid eighth-note multiples. Then:
   - `null90` = the 90th percentile of the null;
   - `matched_med` = the median mel where wave > 0.6, or the 75th percentile of active mel if there are 10 or fewer
     such frames;
   - `thr = null90 + 0.4 × (matched_med − null90)`.
5. **A frame matches** when it is active and wave ≥ 0.4 or mel ≥ thr.
6. **Divergence** is the first 300 ms stretch (at least 60% active, under 30% matched, starting on an unmatched frame)
   that never recovers with a 400 ms matched run. Short dips that recover are dips, not cuts. With no such stretch,
   voice at least 80 ms after the last match counts as divergence. `synced_until` = the last matched frame minus 42 ms
   (one frame at 24 fps).
7. **In-sync spans** are matched voice, bridged across silences and across up to 0.25 s of unmatched voice. Drop spans
   shorter than 0.5 s.
8. Map everything to song time: `song time = song_t0 + clip time − lag`.

The **diagnostic image** shows our vocal's spectrogram with word labels, the take's own soundtrack, the match curves
with the threshold, and the cross-similarity matrix, whose diagonal means "in sync". The **review video** lays our
audio over the take, marked IN SYNC up to the cut and DIVERGED — CUT HERE after it. Look at both before trusting a
number.

**The NCC is a diagnostic, not the verdict.** Over a whole take it is usually 0.1–0.3, because the copy stops somewhere.
One take scored 0.157 and still held 99% of its sung seconds. Measure the lag per take, never as a constant: takes ran
from −0.40 s to +0.83 s. Motion clips conditioned on the mix aren't copied (NCC about 0.05–0.08): play them at lag 0.

**Done when** each take has its spans and its cut, and the review video agrees with them by eye.

**A re-sung soundtrack can still be in sync.** With WHITEPILL's vocal-stem method
([tool 46](#46-lip-sync-from-the-songs-own-vocal)) the check called the first take's soundtrack re-sung rather than copied,
matched only from 7 s on, yet its singing sat exactly where the vocal is, and the director called the take perfect. For
that method, the review video is the verdict: the take with the song laid over, by eye.

**Or align the take, and follow the path.** FABLE aligned each take's own soundtrack to its window by subsequence DTW on
log-mel frames, phrase by phrase, and the cut followed the path: a clean copy costs 0.05–0.2, a re-sung line 0.2–0.4
([tool 81](#81-sync-as-a-path-each-take-aligned-to-its-window)).

![The sync check on an early ESCAPE VELOCITY test: the vocal that was sent, the soundtrack that came back, and how closely they match over time.](https://claudiagallery.vip/record/escape-velocity/lipsync-check.webp)

### 16. Covers and coverage

**The earlier method.** Takes from the song's own vocal stem needed no covers: a take that fails is made again from
better inputs ([tool 46](#46-lip-sync-from-the-songs-own-vocal)), one take per job.

**Job.** Keep the in-sync part of every take, cover the rest, and know how much of the singing is really synced.

**The cut.** Cut on the last eighth note at or before `synced_until`. Eighths are the beat map's beats plus the midpoints
between them. A cut on an eighth feels like part of the music; a cut at the divergence frame looks like a glitch.

**A cover** is a new clip:

- **Window:** it starts in the word gap before the cut, and lasts `clamp(ceil(end − start + 0.3), 4, 8)` whole seconds.
- **Start image:** the parent take's frame at the cut (clip time = cut − `song_t0` + lag), unaltered, sent as the image
  reference, never as a first frame.
- **Words and audio:** exactly the words that start in its window, with their clean vocal.
- **Prompt:** the parent's prompt, re-quoted to the new words.
- **Records:** the parent lists its covers; the cover records its parent and why.
- **Limits:** at most two covers per root, and one on a provider where copies are rare.

**Coverage**, per chain (a root and its covers):

- sung stretches = each aligned word ± 30 ms, merged when closer than 0.12 s;
- in-sync spans = every element's spans, each start extended by 60 ms;
- gaps = sung time not covered by any span, of 0.6 s or more, merged when closer than 0.3 s.

The bar is "most lips", like a pop video ("like grimes vids … shedoesnt sync lips on everything, just most"). Target at
least 80% of sung seconds, never an out-of-sync mouth held on screen, and budget covers at about 60% of the sung
seconds.

**Measured:**

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| ESCAPE VELOCITY | 41% of sung takes copied; with covers, about 86% of sung seconds verified |
| CLODYSSEY, Higgsfield | about 21% of sung takes copied |
| BLISS | 62% of six windows' sung seconds |
| A later test run, seven windows | long prompts held 44% of the chorus's sung seconds; short ones 62–71% |

**When a window won't copy**, try these in order:

1. **The short sung form,** for a clean window. The biggest lever measured there is prompt length. Long timestamped
   screenplays make the model perform the text and re-sing it; short prompts copy. (Takes from the song's own vocal stem
   copy with full prompts of about 200–400 words: [tool 46](#46-lip-sync-from-the-songs-own-vocal).) The short form is:
   - the head, quoting every word;
   - one line of framing and light;
   - at most two timed beats;
   - "One continuous shot, no cuts, no head turns. Only she sings. No text, letters or logos.";
   - about 90 words or fewer.

   On seven windows the mean in-sync share per take went from 26% to 58%; one window went from 0% to 78%. Screenplays
   stay the rule for acting and motion clips.
2. **Clear the mouth.** Nothing in front of it on the plate: no held microphone, hand or hair.
3. **The other provider,** after two non-copies in the short form.
4. **Cut away:** to the shot's motion clip, stills in rhythm, depth moves, crops to the eyes, hair or hands, inserts, or
   a wider or profile framing. The words stay on screen either way.

**No lip-sync models.** Sync, LatentSync and Wav2Lip were tried as fallbacks and dropped: "still not exact", and the
mouths came out forced and glitchy. The failure was the input, not the model.

## The edit and the renderer

### 17. The edit list

**Job.** Resolve every moment of every shot to a source.

**How.** Resolve a sung shot moment by moment in song time. At each time T, use the chain element whose in-sync span
contains T, at clip time `T − song_t0 + lag`. A take and its covers then interleave, each switch sitting on the eighth
before a divergence. Fill holes from the shot's motion clip, then from the plate. Motion clips play straight through,
holding their last frame if the shot is longer.

**Done when** the film renders end to end at every stage, with plates standing in for clips that don't exist yet.
